calls.prompt:
Company: Brightside Foods Co.

US mid-size packaged food company (~900 employees, plants in Ohio and Georgia). Makes hot dogs and sausages, brightly colored gummy candy, and pecan-and-apple snack bars. Buys pecans, apples and corn from US farms. Sells through grocery chains and convenience stores (many customers pay with SNAP / food stamps). Runs its own fleet of 40 delivery trucks. No restaurants, no alcohol, no exports.

Rules that APPLY:
- FDA food additive and color additive rules (dyes in candy, casings, meat)
- Food labeling and food safety rules for packaged food and meat products
- EPA pesticide residue limits on crops we buy (pecans, apples, corn)
- USDA marketing orders and grading for pecans and apples
- SNAP rules that change what shoppers can buy or who qualifies (affects demand)
- Workplace safety and labor rules for food plants; trucking safety rules for our fleet

Rules that DO NOT apply:
- Aviation, airspace, aircraft airworthiness
- Banking, securities, crypto, sanctions
- Medicare/Medicaid payment rules, medical devices
- Mining, offshore oil and gas, fisheries
- Broadcast/TV licensing

Affected areas and owners:
- food-safety: Additives, dyes, labeling, food safety → Maria Chen (Food Safety & Regulatory)
- sourcing: Ingredients from farms, pesticide limits, crop rules → Tom Alvarez (Sourcing)
- sales: Retail channels, SNAP, pricing → Aisha Grant (Sales Compliance)
- operations: Plant safety, labor, trucking fleet → Ben Kowalski (Operations)

Task: Find every US Federal Register document published between 2026-11-09 and 2026-11-13 (inclusive) that affects this company. For each, give the Federal Register document number, title, federalregister.gov URL, the key deadline, a tier (Critical if a deadline is < 90 days from 2026-11-13, otherwise High/Medium/Low by importance), the owner area, a one-line reason, and a one-line action. Only include items you found via search. Return an empty list if none.

Found **9 company-relevant documents**. Dates below are assessed from **2026-11-13**; “Critical—immediate” denotes an obligation already in effect.

1. **FR Doc. 2026-23112 — [Revocation of the Color Additive Listing for Use of Orange B on Casings or Surfaces of Frankfurters and Sausages; Confirmation of Effective Date](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/11/13/2026-23112/revocation-of-the-color-additive-listing-for-use-of-orange-b-on-casings-or-surfaces-of-frankfurters)**  
   **Published:** 2026-11-13 | **Key deadline:** Effective **2026-09-08**, now confirmed | **Tier:** **Critical—immediate**  
   **Owner:** food-safety — Maria Chen  
   **Reason:** FDA confirmed that Orange B is no longer authorized on frankfurter or sausage casings/surfaces, directly affecting Brightside’s meat products.  
   **Action:** Immediately verify formulas, casing specifications, supplier declarations and inventory; remove and document disposition of any Orange B-containing materials.

2. **FR Doc. 2026-22866 — [Color Additive Petition From the International Association of Color Manufacturers; Request To Amend the Color Additive Regulations To Remove the Solvents Methylene Chloride, Trichloroethylene, and Ethylene Dichloride](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/11/10/2026-22866/color-additive-petition-from-the-international-association-of-color-manufacturers-request-to-amend)**  
   **Published:** 2026-11-10 | **Key deadline:** Objections/hearing requests due **2026-12-10**; order scheduled effective **2027-01-11** | **Tier:** **Critical**  
   **Owner:** food-safety — Maria Chen  
   **Reason:** The order removes authorization for these solvents in manufacturing annatto extract, paprika oleoresin and turmeric oleoresin used as food colors.  
   **Action:** Obtain supplier manufacturing declarations, revise color specifications and qualify compliant replacements before the effective date; file any justified objection by December 10.

3. **FR Doc. 2026-22865 — [Color Additive Petition From Environmental Defense Fund et al.; Request To Amend the Color Additive Regulations To Remove the Solvents Ethylene Dichloride, Methylene Chloride, and Trichloroethylene](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/11/10/2026-22865/color-additive-petition-from-environmental-defense-fund-et-al-request-to-amend-the-color-additive)**  
   **Published:** 2026-11-10 | **Key deadline:** Objections/hearing requests due **2026-12-10**; order scheduled effective **2027-01-11** | **Tier:** **Critical**  
   **Owner:** food-safety — Maria Chen  
   **Reason:** This companion order separately removes methylene chloride as a diluent in color-additive mixtures used in fruit-and-vegetable marking inks.  
   **Action:** Check produce and color-ink suppliers for the affected use and incorporate its removal into the FR Doc. 2026-22866 compliance review.

4. **FR Doc. 2026-22944 — [Modification to Work Requirements for Able-Bodied Adults](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/11/10/2026-22944/modification-to-work-requirements-for-able-bodied-adults)**  
   **Published:** 2026-11-10 | **Key deadline:** Comments due **2026-12-10** | **Tier:** **Critical**  
   **Owner:** sales — Aisha Grant  
   **Reason:** Proposed SNAP time-limit exceptions, age coverage and geographic-waiver changes could alter customer eligibility and SNAP-supported demand.  
   **Action:** Model Ohio/Georgia sales exposure under the proposed eligibility scenarios and submit demand-impact comments by December 10.

5. **FR Doc. 2026-22936 — [Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program: Reforming Categorical Eligibility](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/11/10/2026-22936/supplemental-nutrition-assistance-program-reforming-categorical-eligibility)**  
   **Published:** 2026-11-10 | **Key deadline:** Comments due **2026-12-10** | **Tier:** **Critical**  
   **Owner:** sales — Aisha Grant  
   **Reason:** Limiting categorical SNAP eligibility to households receiving TANF “assistance” could remove eligibility based only on noncash or in-kind benefits, reducing the potential customer base.  
   **Action:** Estimate affected SNAP-volume exposure with retail partners and file comments on anticipated demand effects by December 10.

6. **FR Doc. 2026-22826 — [Pecans Grown in the States of Alabama, Arkansas, Arizona, California, Florida, Georgia, Kansas, Louisiana, Missouri, Mississippi, North Carolina, New Mexico, Oklahoma, South Carolina, and Texas; Changes to Membership and Handling Requirements](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/11/09/2026-22826/pecans-grown-in-the-states-of-alabama-arkansas-arizona-california-florida-georgia-kansas-louisiana)**  
   **Published:** 2026-11-09 | **Key deadline:** Comments due **2026-12-09** | **Tier:** **Critical**  
   **Owner:** sourcing — Tom Alvarez  
   **Reason:** Proposed pecan marketing-order changes to handler reporting, inter-handler transfers and assessment late fees could affect supplier administration and costs.  
   **Action:** Confirm which pecan suppliers are regulated handlers, assess contract/cost implications and coordinate any industry comments by December 9.

7. **FR Doc. 2026-22761 — [Rules of Practice and Procedure for Administrative Hearings Before the Office of Administrative Law Judges](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/11/09/2026-22761/rules-of-practice-and-procedure-for-administrative-hearings-before-the-office-of-administrative-law)**  
   **Published:** 2026-11-09 | **Key deadline:** Effective **2026-12-09** | **Tier:** **Critical**  
   **Owner:** operations — Ben Kowalski  
   **Reason:** Represented parties in Department of Labor OALJ proceedings must generally use electronic filing and service, affecting any future OSHA, wage or other covered labor dispute.  
   **Action:** Have labor counsel establish eFile/eServe readiness and update litigation procedures by December 9; no plant-wide process change is otherwise needed.

8. **FR Doc. 2026-22814 — [Agency Information Collection Activities: Requests for Comments; Clearance of a Renewed Approval of Information Collection(s): Procedures for Transportation Workplace Drug and Alcohol Testing Programs (ICR 2105-0529)](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/11/09/2026-22814/agency-information-collection-activities-requests-for-comments-clearance-of-a-renewed-approval-of)**  
   **Published:** 2026-11-09 | **Key deadline:** Comments due **2027-01-08** | **Tier:** **Critical** *(deadline-driven; routine renewal)*  
   **Owner:** operations — Ben Kowalski  
   **Reason:** The renewal covers DOT Part 40 drug/alcohol-testing records and MIS/alcohol-testing forms relevant to FMCSA-regulated fleet employers.  
   **Action:** Verify the fleet’s testing records and forms remain current and submit comments by January 8 only if the renewal’s burden estimates or proposed form revisions raise issues.

9. **FR Doc. 2026-22891 — [Rules and Regulations, Series 8](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/11/10/2026-22891/rules-and-regulations-series-8)**  
   **Published:** 2026-11-10 | **Key deadline:** No new general compliance deadline; a covered NLRB petition response remains due **14 days after service** | **Tier:** **Low**  
   **Owner:** operations — Ben Kowalski  
   **Reason:** This technical correction revises and reinstates NLRB procedures at 29 CFR 102.101–102.103 but creates no new substantive plant obligation.  
   **Action:** No immediate action; have labor counsel reference the corrected provisions if an NLRB jurisdictional advisory-opinion petition arises.

*Scope check:* The EPA tolerance actions found in this window concerned **fig** and **sunflower**, not Brightside’s purchased pecans, apples or corn, so they are not included.

###### Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration

1. [Docket No. FMCSA-2026-0036]

# AGENCY:

Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration (FMCSA), Department of Transportation (DOT).

# ACTION:

Notice of denials.

# SUMMARY:

FMCSA announces its decision to deny applications from 16 individuals who requested an exemption from the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Regulations (FMCSRs) prohibiting persons with a clinical diagnosis of epilepsy or any other condition that is likely to cause a loss of consciousness or any loss of ability to operate a commercial motor vehicle (CMV) from operating CMVs in interstate commerce.

...

## III. Background

 The physical qualification standard for drivers regarding seizures and loss of consciousness provides that a person is physically qualified to drive a CMV if that person has “no established medical history or clinical diagnosis of epilepsy or any other condition which is likely to cause the loss of consciousness or any loss of ability to control” a CMV (49 CFR 391.41(b)(8)). To assist in applying this standard, FMCSA publishes guidance for medical examiners (MEs) in the form of medical advisory criteria in Appendix A to 49 CFR part 391. [1] In 2007, FMCSA published recommendations from a Medical Expert Panel (MEP) that FMCSA tasked to review the existing seizure disorder guidelines for MEs. [2] The MEP performed a comprehensive, systematic literature review, including evidence available at the time. The MEP issued recommended criteria to evaluate whether an individual with a history of epilepsy, a single unprovoked seizure, or a provoked seizure should be allowed to drive a CMV. 

On January 15, 2013, FMCSA began granting exemptions, on a case-by-case basis, to individual drivers from the physical qualification standard regarding seizures and loss of consciousness in 49 CFR 391.41(b)(8) (78 FR 3069). The Agency considers the medical advisory criteria, the 2007 MEP recommendations, and each individual's medical information and driving record in deciding whether to grant the exemption.

On March 17, 2026, FMCSA published a notice announcing receipt of applications from 17 individuals requesting an exemption from the epilepsy and seizure disorders prohibition in 49 CFR 391.41(b)(8) and requested comments from the public (91 FR 12893). The public comment period ended on April 16, 2026, and five comments were received.

## IV. Discussion of Comments

FMCSA received five comments on these exemption applications. One commenter advocated balanced and individualized regulations that prioritize both public safety and the equal opportunity for individuals to drive when their seizures are well-managed. In response to this comment, FMCSA finds that its seizure exemption process adequately balances the Agency's mission of improving public safety on the nation's roadways with the opportunity for otherwise ineligible individuals to present evidence of why they should nonetheless be permitted to drive CMVs.

...

## V. Basis for Exemption Determination

 The Agency conducted an individualized assessment of each applicant's medical information, including the root cause of the respective seizure(s) and medical information about the applicant's seizure history, the length of time that has elapsed since the individual's last seizure, the stability of each individual's treatment regimen, and the duration of time on or off of anti-seizure medication. In addition, the Agency reviewed the treating clinician's medical opinion related to the ability of the driver to safely operate a CMV with a seizure history and each applicant's certified driving record from their State Driver Licensing Agency (SDLA). The information obtained from each applicant's driving record provides the Agency with details regarding any moving violations or reported crash data, which demonstrates whether the driver has a safe driving history and is an indicator of future driving performance. If the driving record revealed a crash, FMCSA requested and reviewed the related police reports and other relevant documents, such as the citation and conviction information. A summary of each applicant's seizure history was discussed in the March 17, 2026, Federal Register notice (91 FR 12893) and will not be repeated in this notice. 

## VI. Conclusion

Based upon its evaluation of the 17 exemption applications, FMCSA has determined that the following 16 applicants do not satisfy the eligibility criteria or meet the terms and conditions of the Federal exemption and granting these exemptions would not provide a level of safety that would be equivalent to, or greater than, the level of safety that would be obtained by complying with 49 CFR 391.41(b)(8). Therefore, the 16 applicants in this notice have been denied exemptions from the physical qualification standards in 49 CFR 391.41(b)(8).

Each applicant has, prior to this notice, received a letter of final disposition regarding his or her exemption request. Those decision letters fully outlined the basis for the denial and constitute final action by the Agency. This notice summarizes the Agency's recent denials as required under 49 U.S.C. 31315(b)(6)(c) by publishing names and reasons for denial.

The following 16 applicants do not meet the minimum time requirement for being seizure-free, either on or off anti-seizure medication:

Andrew Barker (NC)

Kyle Benner (PA)

Devin Brockington (MD)

Wendy Cook (OR)

Caedmon Cunningham (KS)

Steven Ernest (ME)

Chauncy Gibson (GA)

Matthew Heller (NY)

Michael S. Miller (CA)

Michael George Murray (NY)

Brandon Petruzzi (MA)

Scott Pontious (OH)

Anthony Sanders (MO)

Ryen Seyfried (NY)

Jeffrey Sparkman (KY)

Donte Watkins (NC)

Larry W. Minor,

Associate Administrator for Policy.

# AGENCY:

Food and Nutrition Administration (FNA), USDA.

# ACTION:

Proposed rule.

# SUMMARY:

Under section 5(a) of the Food and Nutrition Act of 2008, households in which each member receives benefits under a State program funded by Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF) are categorically eligible for the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP). Current SNAP regulations consider TANF benefits to include both cash assistance and non-cash or in-kind benefits or services from TANF-funded programs. This proposal would limit categorical eligibility to only households that receive TANF assistance, as defined at 45 CFR 260.31. These revisions would ensure that SNAP benefits are targeted to needy households that have qualified for TANF assistance while still aligning categorical eligibility's statutory purpose of simplifying program administration.

The proposed rule would remove 7 CFR 273.2(j)(2)(i)(B), (2)(i)(C), and (2)(ii), meaning States would no longer be permitted to confer categorical eligibility for SNAP to households that receive non-cash or in-kind TANF- or State MOE-funded benefits or services, other than TANF assistance. This would eliminate the practice of States using nominal TANF benefits from programs with a variety of weaker gross income and resource limits to confer categorical eligibility.

Federal Register :: Respirable Crystalline Silica and Respiratory Protection 

# Respirable Crystalline Silica and Respiratory Protection 

 A Proposed Rule by the Mine Safety and Health Administration on 11/12/2026 

 This document has a comment period that ends in 52 days. (01/11/2027) Submit a public comment 

 Thank you for taking the time to create a comment. Your input is important. 

 Once you have filled in the required fields below you can preview and/or submit your comment to the Labor Department for review. All comments are considered public and will be posted online once the Labor Department has reviewed them. 

 You can view alternative ways to comment or you may also comment via Regulations.gov at https://www.regulations.gov/commenton/MSHA-2026-0200-0001. 

- Document Details Document Details

Published Content - Document Details

Document Headings

 Document headings vary by document type but may contain the following: 

1. the agency or agencies that issued and signed a document 
2. the number of the CFR title and the number of each part the document amends, proposes to amend, or is directly related to 
3. the agency docket number / agency internal file number 
4. the RIN which identifies each regulatory action listed in the Unified Agenda of Federal Regulatory and Deregulatory Actions 

 See the Document Drafting Handbook for more details. 

###### Mine Safety and Health Administration

1. 30 CFR Parts 56, 57, 60, 71, and 72
2. [Docket No. MSHA-2026-0200]
3. RIN 1219-AC22

# AGENCY:

Mine Safety and Health Administration (MSHA), Department of Labor.

# ACTION:

Proposed rule, request for comments; notice of public hearing.

# SUMMARY:

 This proposed rule clarifies and modifies provisions of the respirable crystalline silica and respiratory protection standards that were established in MSHA's 2024 final rule titled “ Lowering Miners' Exposure to Respirable Crystalline Silica and Improving Respiratory Protection.” The changes provide clarity and make improvements to the requirements for methods of compliance, exposure monitoring, respiratory protection, medical surveillance, and recordkeeping while maintaining strong protection of miners. The proposal also includes related conforming amendments. 

# DATES:

 Written Comments. Written comments must be received or postmarked by midnight Eastern Time on January 11, 2027. 

 Public Hearing. MSHA will hold a virtual-only public hearing on December 15, 2026. For more information on the public hearing, see SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION . 

# ADDRESSES:

All submissions must include RIN 1219-AC22 or Docket No. MSHA-2026-0200. You should not include personal or proprietary information that you do not wish to disclose publicly. If you mark parts of a comment as “business confidential” information, MSHA will not post those parts of the comment. Otherwise, MSHA will post all comments without change, including any personal information provided. MSHA cautions against submitting personal information.

You may submit comments and informational materials, clearly identified by RIN 1219-AC22 or Docket No. MSHA-2026-0200, by any of the following methods:

 1. Federal E-Rulemaking Portal: https://www.regulations.gov. Follow the online instructions for submitting comments for MSHA-2026-0200. A plain language summary of the rule is also available on the Federal E-Rulemaking Portal. 

 2. Email: zzMSHA-comments@dol.gov. Include “RIN 1219-AC22” in the subject line of the message. 

 3. Regular Mail or Hand Delivery: MSHA, Office of Standards, Regulations, and Variances, 200 Constitution Avenue NW, Washington, DC 20210. Before visiting MSHA in person, call 202-693-9440 to make an appointment. No telefacsimiles (“faxes”) will be accepted. 

# FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:

 Corliss A. Josephs-Conway, Acting Director, Office of Standards, Regulations, and Variances, MSHA at MSHARulemaking@dol.gov (email) or 202-693-9440 (voice). This is not a toll-free number. 

# SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:

MSHA will hold a virtual-only public hearing to provide industry, labor, and other interested parties with an opportunity to present oral statements, written comments, and other information on the proposed rule. The virtual-only public hearing will begin at 9 a.m. Eastern Time on December 15, 2026. If necessary, the hearing will continue on December 16, 2026.

The virtual-only public hearing will begin with an opening statement from MSHA, followed by an opportunity for members of the public to make oral presentations. Speakers and other attendees may present information to MSHA for inclusion in the rulemaking record. The hearing will be conducted in an informal manner. Formal rules of evidence or cross examination will not apply.

 A verbatim transcript of the proceeding will be prepared and made a part of the rulemaking record. A copy of the transcript will be available to the public. MSHA will make the transcript of the hearing available at http://www.regulations.gov.

MSHA will accept post-hearing written comments and other appropriate information for the record from any interested party, including those not presenting oral statements, received by midnight Eastern Time on January 11, 2027.

 Pre-registration is not required to attend the hearing. Additional information on how to attend the virtual-only public hearing will be available at https://www.msha.gov/​regulations/​rulemaking/​silica-public-hearing-information.

 Those who wish to speak during the virtual public hearing are encouraged to register in advance at https://www.msha.gov/​regulations/​rulemaking/​public-hearing-information. Speakers will be called in the order in which they signed up. Those who do not register in advance will have an opportunity to speak after all those who pre-registered have spoken. You may submit hearing testimony and documentary evidence, identified by docket number (MSHA-2026-0200), by any of the methods previously identified. 

The preamble to the proposed rule follows this outline:

I. Introduction

II. Background

III. Request for Comments

IV. Section-by-Section Analysis

V. Health Effects Summary

VI. Preliminary Risk Analysis

VII. Preliminary Regulatory Impact Analysis

VIII. Regulatory Alternatives

IX. Regulatory Flexibility Analysis

X. Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995

XI. Other Regulatory Considerations

XII. References

## I. Introduction

 The purpose of this proposed rule is to provide clarity and make improvements to the requirements established in the April 18, 2024, final rule “ Lowering Miners' Exposure to Respirable Crystalline Silica and Improving Respiratory Protection” (2024 Silica Final Rule, 89 FR 28218). The proposed rule includes clarifications and improvements to requirements for methods of compliance, exposure monitoring, respiratory protection, medical surveillance, and recordkeeping while maintaining the protection of miners. The proposal also includes related conforming amendments. 

After the 2024 Silica Final Rule's publication, MSHA held seven stakeholder meetings fielding questions from the public and received stakeholder emails asking questions regarding implementation of MSHA's silica requirements. Many stakeholders asked for clarification on interpreting the restriction on the rotation of miners to comply with the silica permissible exposure limit (PEL) under § 60.11 in title 30 of the Code of Federal Regulations (30 CFR). MSHA is proposing changes to the requirements in § 60.11 to clarify when rotation of miners is permitted for miners exposed to respirable crystalline silica.

Additionally, many stakeholders asked on what basis MSHA would issue citations for silica sample results that exceed the PEL. Stakeholders also asked how MSHA would consider error in silica sample results after the Agency determined it would not include a specific error factor in the 2024 Silica Final Rule.

 When developing the 2024 Silica Final Rule, MSHA anticipated variability in silica sample results because MSHA provided operators with ( printed page 73063) the flexibility to choose from multiple commercially available particle size-selective samplers that conform to the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) 7708:1995(E) standard “ Air quality—Particle size fraction definitions for health-related sampling.” from multiple analytical methods, and from third-party laboratories accredited to the ISO/International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC) 17025 standard “ General requirements for the competence of testing and calibration laboratories.” This flexibility allowed mine operators to select sampling equipment, analytical methods, and laboratories that meet their business needs; to avoid equipment availability constraints; and to ensure they receive timely and accurate results needed to protect miners from silica overexposure. 

Since the 2024 Silica Final Rule's publication, MSHA reviewed mine operators' and MSHA inspectors' sample results. The review demonstrated consistency across respirable crystalline silica samples taken by MSHA inspectors and more variability across respirable crystalline silica samples taken by mine operators. MSHA is proposing to add a single, uniform error factor adjustment of 21 percent to its standards that would be applied to both MSHA sample results and operators' sample results to determine noncompliance with the PEL or exposure at or above the action level. Additionally, MSHA is proposing that only MSHA samples would be the basis for issuing citations for noncompliance with the PEL because MSHA can ensure accuracy across inspectors' samples with a high level of confidence.

The Agency does not think it is feasible to develop an error factor for each operator sample because mine operators may use any combination of the multiple commercially available particle size-selective samplers, various analytical methods, and different third-party laboratories that meet the requirements of 30 CFR part 60 (Part 60); therefore, each combination would require a separate and unique error factor. As a result, MSHA is proposing to allow operators to apply the same error factor adjustment of 21 percent to their sample results for consistency. Mine operators would use their sample results to determine if silica exposure levels at their mines require them to take action to protect miners from respirable crystalline silica overexposures.

Based on updated analysis and stakeholder comments, MSHA is also proposing other changes to improve exposure monitoring for respirable crystalline silica, to clarify when metal and nonmetal (MNM) mine operators may use respirators, and to adopt the Occupational Safety and Health Administration's (OSHA's) Respiratory Protection Standard which would improve safety for miners when wearing respirators voluntarily.

MSHA is also proposing changes to its medical surveillance requirements to address the potential for constraints on the capacity of NIOSH-certified B Readers for medical examinations due to limitations in multi-state support and expected growth in the number of MNM mines for critical minerals. The proposal would update medical surveillance requirements to be more risk-based, which would provide relevant medical information to those miners (both MNM and coal) at risk of material impairment of health or functional capacity from overexposure to respirable crystalline silica. Other proposed changes to medical surveillance would improve access for MNM miners to obtain voluntary medical examinations and remove the requirement for mine operators to ensure the results of chest X-ray classifications are provided to the National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH).

Additionally, MSHA is proposing changes to the recordkeeping requirements under Part 60 to be consistent with proposed changes elsewhere and is proposing other conforming amendments in 30 CFR parts 56, 57, 71, and 72.

 Finally, MSHA is not proposing any changes to the respirable crystalline silica PEL, for all miners, of 50 micrograms per cubic meter of air (µg/m 3 ) for a full-shift exposure, or the action level of 25 µg/m 3 for a full-shift exposure, both calculated as an 8-hour time-weighted average (TWA), established in the 2024 Silica Final Rule. The changes from the 2024 Silica Final Rule that are proposed would clarify and improve mine operators' compliance requirements for respirable crystalline silica overexposure and improve respiratory protections and health protections for all miners. All references in this proposal to the “existing rule” refer to the provisions established in the 2024 Silica Final Rule. 

## II. Background

### A. Pertinent Legal Authority

The statutory authority for this proposed rule is provided by the Federal Mine Safety and Health Act of 1977, as amended (Mine Act) under sections 101(a), 103(h), and 508. 30 U.S.C. 811(a), 813(h), and 957. MSHA implements the provisions of the Mine Act to prevent death, illness, and injury from mining and promote safe and healthful workplaces for miners. The Mine Act requires the Secretary of Labor (Secretary) to develop and promulgate improved mandatory health or safety standards to prevent hazardous and unhealthful conditions and protect the health and safety of the nation's miners. 30 U.S.C. 811(a).

 Congress passed the Mine Act to address these dangers, finding “an urgent need to provide more effective means and measures for improving the working conditions and practices in the Nation's coal or other mines in order to prevent death and serious physical harm, and in order to prevent occupational diseases originating in such mines.” 30 U.S.C. 801(c). Congress concluded that “the existence of unsafe and unhealthful conditions and practices in the Nation's coal or other mines is a serious impediment to the future growth of the coal or other mining industry and cannot be tolerated.” 30 U.S.C. 801(d). Accordingly, “the Mine Act evinces a clear bias in favor of miner health and safety.” Nat'l Mining Ass'n v. Sec'y, U.S. Dep't of Lab., 812 F.3d 843, 866 (11th Cir. 2016). 

 Section 101(a) of the Mine Act gives the Secretary the authority to develop, promulgate, and revise mandatory health standards to address toxic materials or harmful physical agents. 30 U.S.C. 811(a). Under Section 101(a), a standard must protect lives and prevent injuries in mines and be “improved” over any standard that it replaces or revises. Id. Additionally, Section 101(a)(9) prohibits the Secretary from promulgating a mandatory health or safety standard that reduces the protection afforded miners by an existing mandatory health or safety standard. 30 U.S.C. 811(a)(9). Section 101(a)(9) is also known as the “no-less protection rule,” and courts have noted that “Section 101(a)(9) requires the agency to state the basis for its conclusion that the rule has been satisfied,” but judicial “review of that substantive determination is, as always, `highly deferential and presumes the validity of agency action.”' Nat'l Min. Ass'n v. Mine Safety & Health Admin., 116 F.3d 520, 535, 536 (D.C. Cir. 1997) (quoting United Mine Workers of Am., Int'l Union v. Dole, 870 F.2d 662, 666 (D.C. Cir. 1989)). Section 101(a) of the Mine Act also authorizes the Secretary to “prescribe the type and frequency of medical examinations or other tests which shall be made available, by the operator at his cost, to miners exposed ( printed page 73064) to such hazards in order to most effectively determine whether the health of such miners is adversely affected by such exposure.” 30 U.S.C. 811(a)(7). 

 The Secretary must set standards to assure, based on the best available evidence, that no miner will suffer material impairment of health or functional capacity from exposure to toxic materials or harmful physical agents over their working lives. 30 U.S.C. 811(a)(6)(A). In developing standards that attain the “highest degree of health and safety protection for the miner,” the Mine Act requires that the Secretary consider the latest available scientific data in the field, the feasibility of the standards, and experience gained under the Mine Act and other health and safety laws. Id. As a result, courts have found it “appropriate to `give an extreme degree of deference'” to MSHA “`when it is evaluating scientific data within its technical expertise.'” Nat'l Mining Ass'n, 812 F.3d at 866 (quoting Kennecott Greens Creek Mining Co. v. MSHA, 476 F.3d 946, 954 (D.C. Cir. 2007)). Consequently, MSHA's “duty to use the best evidence and to consider feasibility . . . cannot be wielded as counterweight to MSHA's overarching role to protect the life and health of workers in the mining industry.” Id. Thus, “when MSHA itself weighs the evidence before it, it does so in light of its congressional mandate” in favor of protecting miners' health. Id. Moreover, “the Mine Act does not contain the `significant risk' threshold requirement” from the OSH Act. Nat'l Mining Ass'n v. United Steel Workers, 985 F.3d 1309, 1319 (11th Cir. 2021); see also Nat'l Min. Ass'n v. Mine Safety & Health Admin., 116 F.3d 520, 527-28 (D.C. Cir. 1997) (contrasting the Mine Act at 30 U.S.C. 811(a) with the OSH Act at 29 U.S.C. 652 and noting that “[a]rguably, this language does not mandate the same risk-finding requirement as OSHA” and holding that “[a]t most, . . . [MSHA] was required to identify a significant risk associated with having no [relevant] standard at all”). 

 Section 103(h) of the Mine Act gives the Secretary the authority to promulgate standards involving recordkeeping and reporting. 30 U.S.C. 813(h). Additionally, section 103(h) requires that every mine operator establish and maintain records, make reports, and provide this information as required by the Secretary. Id. Section 508 of the Mine Act gives the Secretary the authority to issue regulations to carry out any provision of the Mine Act. 30 U.S.C. 957. 

### B. Regulatory History

 On April 18, 2024, MSHA published the 2024 Silica Final Rule (89 FR 28218). The standalone documents, “ Effects of Occupational Exposure to Respirable Crystalline Silica on the Health of Miners,” “ Final Risk Analysis,” and “ Final Regulatory Impact Analysis,” were also made publicly available at that time. MSHA set the PEL of respirable crystalline silica at 50 µg/m 3 for a full-shift exposure, calculated as an 8-hour TWA. The 2024 Silica Final Rule included other requirements for sampling, qualitative evaluations, corrective actions, and medical surveillance for MNM mines, and also included new requirements for respiratory protection, including the incorporation by reference of ASTM International (ASTM) F3387-19, Standard Practice for Respiratory Protection. 

The final rule took effect on June 17, 2024. Compliance with the final rule was scheduled for April 14, 2025, for coal mine operators and April 8, 2026, for MNM mine operators. Following publication of the final rule, industry groups, including the National Stone, Sand and Gravel Association (NSSGA); the Sorptive Minerals Institute (SMI); and others, filed petitions in the United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit, asserting concerns regarding the rule's feasibility, control methods, and sampling requirements. On April 11, 2025, the Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals issued an order staying the 2024 Silica Final Rule's compliance deadlines until the Court completes a substantive review of the petition. In accordance with the judicial directive, MSHA continues to temporarily pause enforcement of the requirements in the 2024 Silica Final Rule for mine operators.

### C. Developments Affecting MSHA's Provisions on Exposure Monitoring

In the 2024 Silica Final Rule, MSHA discussed its decision not to include an error factor for respirable crystalline silica sample results in its standards in response to several comments recommending the adoption of one (89 FR 28317). Commenters recommended that the PEL (30 CFR 60.10) and action level (30 CFR 60.2) should have an error factor to account for sampling and analysis errors. One commenter pointed to the 2014 Respirable Coal Mine Dust standard as an example of MSHA applying an error factor to the PEL to normalize results to account for errors in sampling and weighing that cause deviations in individual concentration measurements.

After careful consideration of these comments, MSHA decided not to include an error factor in the 2024 Silica Final Rule and based its findings on the following considerations: (1) there are many sampling devices available that conform to the ISO 7708:1995(E) standard for particle size-selective samplers with an acceptable level of measurement bias, and (2) both the X-Ray Diffraction (XRD) and Infrared Spectroscopy (IR) analytical methods can measure respirable crystalline silica with acceptable precision at amounts that would be collected by samplers when airborne concentrations are at or around the PEL and action level. Even though an error factor was not published in the 2024 Silica Final Rule, MSHA would have applied an error factor to any MSHA sample result, consistent with the NIOSH Accuracy Criterion and MSHA's long-standing practice, to determine whether the result was an overexposure of the PEL. This is similar to how the Agency applies an error factor to MSHA sample results of the P-2 and P-7 analyses for quartz at MNM and coal mines, respectively.

MSHA's decision not to mandate mine operators to use specific samplers or laboratories in the 2024 Silica Final Rule allows for variability among samplers and laboratory analysis methods. MSHA determined that additional restrictions on the types of samplers would create supply issues for operators because there are not enough of any one type of ISO-conforming sampling equipment to meet the sampling needs of all mines and many mine operators already had ISO-conforming sampling equipment that was being used for respirable crystalline silica sampling. Also, mine operators were concerned about facing significant delays in obtaining sample results, an issue which would have been exacerbated if MSHA had limited the laboratories available to operators by mandating that operators use specific ISO-accredited laboratories for sample analysis.

 After publication of the 2024 Silica Final Rule, MSHA continued to receive questions during stakeholder meetings on whether an error factor would be applied to operators' samples. MSHA responded that the Agency, consistent with its practice of applying an error factor to sample results for other health hazards, would apply an error factor to MSHA respirable crystalline silica sample results but did not address whether operator samples for respirable crystalline silica would also have an error factor applied. Since the stakeholder meetings, MSHA observed ( printed page 73065) variability in silica sample results when comparing different combinations of compliant pumps, samplers, laboratories, and analytic methods used. Specifically, the Agency observed more consistent results for MSHA samples, which are based on a single combination of pump, sampler, and laboratory. 

 MSHA is proposing in this rule to cite a violation of the respirable crystalline silica PEL only when the Agency has evidence that a violation occurred based on its own samples. Moreover, MSHA would determine that a violation has occurred when an MSHA sample, including an error factor adjustment of 21 percent, exceeds the PEL. MSHA's error factor model accounts for laboratory analyses variability and other sampling variables for samples taken by MSHA inspectors to ensure the Agency's process for its health standards citations and penalties is in accordance with the NIOSH Accuracy Criterion. [1] The error factor is necessary because when an MSHA sample is challenged, it allows the Secretary to show by a preponderance of the evidence that the sample is above the PEL. 

 MSHA is also proposing to apply an error factor adjustment of 21 percent to operator samples to determine compliance with the requirements of this part and for consistency across all samples, both operator and MSHA samples. While operator samples would not be cited for overexposure, there are still certain actions that operators must take based on their own sampling, such as corrective actions to reduce respirable crystalline silica exposures when sample results are above the PEL. # AGENCY:

Drug Enforcement Administration, Department of Justice.

# ACTION:

Interim final rule; request for comments.

# SUMMARY:

 On August 5, 2026, the United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved a new drug application for Orzeyful (oveporexton) for the treatment of narcolepsy type 1 in adults. The Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) provided the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) with a scheduling recommendation to place oveporexton, chemically known as N -[(2 S, 3 R)-2-[[3-(3,5-difluorophenyl)-2-fluorophenyl]methyl]-4,4-difluoro-1-(2-hydroxy-2-methylpropanoyl)pyrrolidin-3-yl]ethanesulfonamide, in schedule IV of the Controlled Substances Act (CSA). In accordance with the CSA, as amended by the Improving Regulatory Transparency for New Medical Therapies Act, DEA is hereby issuing an interim final rule placing oveporexton, including its salts, isomers and salts of isomers whenever the existence of such salts, isomers, and salts of isomers is possible, in schedule IV of the CSA.

# SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:

In this interim final rule (IFR), Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) is adding oveporexton to schedule IV of the Controlled Substances Act (CSA).

## Posting of Public Comments

 All comments received in response to this docket are considered part of the public record. DEA will make comments available for public inspection online at https://www.regulations.gov, unless reasonable cause is given. Such information includes personal or business identifying information (such as name, address, State or Federal identifiers, etc.) voluntarily submitted by the commenter. 

 Commenters submitting comments which include personal identifying information (PII), confidential, or proprietary business information that the commenter does not want made publicly available should submit two copies of the comment. One copy must be marked “CONTAINS CONFIDENTIAL INFORMATION” and should clearly identify all PII or business information the commenter does not want to be made publicly available, including any supplemental materials. DEA will review this copy, including the claimed PII and confidential business information, in its consideration of comments. The second copy should be marked “TO BE PUBLICLY POSTED” and must have all claimed confidential PII and business information already redacted. DEA will post only the redacted comment on https://www.regulations.gov for public inspection. DEA generally will not redact additional information contained in the comment marked “TO BE PUBLICLY POSTED.” The Freedom of Information Act applies to all comments received. 

 For easy reference, an electronic copy of this document and supplemental information to this IFR are available at http://www.regulations.gov.

## Request for Hearing or Appearance; Waiver

 Pursuant to 21 U.S.C. 811(j)(3), an interested person may “request a hearing.” Such proceedings are conducted pursuant to the provisions of the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), 5 U.S.C. 551-559. [1] Interested persons, as defined in 21 CFR 1300.01(b), may file requests for a hearing in conformity with the requirements of 21 CFR 1308.44(a) and 1316.47(a), and such requests must: 

(1) state with particularity the interest of the person in the proceeding;

(2) state with particularity the objections or issues concerning which the person desires to be heard; and

 (3) state briefly the position of the person with regard to the objections or issues. Any interested person may file a waiver of an opportunity for a hearing or to participate in a hearing in conformity with the requirements of 21 CFR 1308.44(c), together with a written statement of position on the matters of fact and law involved in any hearing. [2] 

 All requests for hearings and waivers of participation, together with a written statement of position on the matters of fact and law involved in such hearing, must be sent to DEA using the address information provided above. The decision whether a hearing will be needed to address such matters of fact and law in the rulemaking will be made by the Administrator. If a hearing is needed, DEA will publish a notice of hearing on the interim final rule in the Federal Register . [3] Further, once the Administrator determines a hearing is needed to address such matters of fact and law in rulemaking, he will then designate an Administrative Law Judge (ALJ) to preside over the hearing. The ALJ's functions shall commence upon designation, as provided in 21 CFR 1316.52. 

In accordance with 21 U.S.C. 811 and 812, the purpose of a hearing would be to determine whether oveporexton meets the statutory criteria for placement in schedule IV.

## Legal Authority

 Under the CSA, as amended in 2015 by the Improving Regulatory Transparency for New Medical Therapies Act (section 2(b) of Pub. L. 114-89), DEA is required to commence an expedited scheduling action with respect to certain new drugs approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA). As provided in 21 U.S.C. 811(j), this expedited scheduling is required where both of the following conditions apply: (1) The Secretary of the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) has advised DEA that a New Drug Application (NDA) has been submitted for a drug that has a ( printed page 72777) stimulant, depressant, or hallucinogenic effect on the central nervous system (CNS), and that it appears that such drug has an abuse potential; and (2) the Secretary of HHS recommends that DEA control the drug in schedule II, III, IV, or V pursuant to 21 U.S.C. 811(a) and (b). In these circumstances, DEA is required to issue an IFR controlling the drug within 90 days. 

 Subsection 811(j)(2) states that the 90-day timeframe starts the later of (1) the date DEA receives HHS's scientific and medical evaluation/scheduling recommendation, or (2) the date DEA receives notice of the NDA approval by HHS. Subsection 811(j)(3) specifies that the rulemaking shall become immediately effective as an IFR without requiring DEA to demonstrate good cause therefore. Thus, the purpose of subsection 811(j) is to speed the process by which DEA schedules newly approved drugs that are currently either in schedule I or not controlled (but which have sufficient abuse potential to warrant control) so that such drugs may be marketed without undue delay following FDA approval. [4] 

Subsection 811(j)(3) further provides that the IFR shall give interested persons the opportunity to comment and to request a hearing. After the conclusion of such proceedings, DEA must issue a final rule in accordance with the scheduling criteria of 21 U.S.C. 811(b) through (d), and 812(b).

## Background

Oveporexton (also known as TAK-861) is a new molecular entity with CNS activity as an orexin type 2 receptor (OX2R) agonist. Selective OX2R agonism is a distinct pharmacological mechanism of action from other substances currently listed in the CSA.

On December 10, 2025, Takeda Pharmaceuticals U.S.A., Inc. (Sponsor) submitted an NDA for oveporexton to FDA. On August 5, 2026, FDA approved the NDA for oveporexton (Orzeyful) for the treatment of narcolepsy type 1 (NT1) in adults. The approved formulation consists of tablets in 0.5 mg, 1 mg, and 2 mg strengths, with a recommended dosage of either 1 mg or 2 mg taken orally twice daily.

## Determination To Schedule Oveporexton

On July 31, 2026, DEA received from HHS a scientific and medical evaluation titled “Basis for the Recommendation to Control Oveporexton in Schedule IV of the Controlled Substances Act” and a scheduling recommendation. Pursuant to 21 U.S.C. 811(b) and (c), this document contained an eight-factor analysis of the abuse potential, legitimate medical use, and dependence liability of oveporexton, along with HHS's recommendation to control oveporexton under schedule IV of the CSA.

In response, DEA reviewed the scientific and medical evaluation and scheduling recommendation provided by HHS, along with all other relevant data, and completed its own eight-factor review pursuant to 21 U.S.C. 811(c). DEA concluded that oveporexton meets the 21 U.S.C. 812(b)(4) criteria for placement in schedule IV of the CSA.

Pursuant to subsection 811(j), and based on HHS's scheduling recommendation, the approval of the NDA by HHS/FDA, and DEA's determination, DEA is issuing this IFR to schedule oveporexton as a schedule IV controlled substance under the CSA.

 Included below is a brief summary of each factor as analyzed by HHS and DEA, and as considered by DEA in its scheduling action. Please note that both DEA and HHS analyses are available in their entirety under “Supporting Documents” in the public docket for this IFR at https://www.regulations.gov, under Docket Number “DEA-1775.” Full analysis of, and citations to, the information referenced in the summary may also be found in the supporting and related material. 

 1. Its Actual or Relative Potential for Abuse: Oveporexton is new molecular entity that has not been marketed legally or illegally in the United States and was recently approved for treatment of NT1 in China and Japan. Given that oveporexton is new to the global market, evidence regarding its diversion, illicit manufacturing, or abuse is currently lacking. FDA is not aware of any diversion from research activities or manufacturing facilities for oveporexton, and DEA's National Forensic Laboratory Information System (NFLIS)-Drug [5] database reflects that oveporexton has not been encountered by law enforcement in the United States. 

 Oveporexton is an OX2R-selective agonist with demonstrated CNS activity. There are currently no OX2R-selective agonists listed in the CSA. In nonclinical studies, oveporexton produces stimulant-like behavioral alterations in rodents and has weak reinforcing effects, as demonstrated by a rat self-administration study. In humans, some potential abuse-related treatment-emergent adverse events involving oveporexton occurred across clinical trials with higher incidence at supratherapeutic doses. Also, a human abuse potential study showed that supratherapeutic doses of oveporexton produced abuse-related subjective effect ratings that were not statistically significantly different from phentermine (schedule IV) ( see Factor 2). Based on these data, oveporexton has a potential for abuse similar to the schedule IV stimulant phentermine, making it reasonable to assume its potential for diversion, misuse, and creating a hazard to the health of individuals or the community will be similar to that of substances in schedule IV of the CSA. 

 2. Scientific Evidence of Its Pharmacological Effects, if Known: The pharmacological effects of oveporexton were assessed using available nonclinical and clinical data. In vitro binding and functional studies demonstrate that oveporexton is a potent and selective OX2R agonist which lacks off-target effects at other receptor targets associated with abuse potential. Animal behavioral studies show that oveporexton has some stimulant-like and reinforcing properties. Oveporexton produced transient stimulant-like behavior in rats, with the most frequent behavioral observation in the modified Irwin's multiple observation method being slight restlessness 1-2 hours after administration of ≥20 mg/kg oral oveporexton. In a drug discrimination study in rats, oveporexton at doses up to 5 mg/kg (orally) did not substitute for the discriminative stimulus of the schedule II stimulant, d -amphetamine (0.3 mg/kg, subcutaneously). A second drug discrimination study revealed that rats could not be trained to discriminate oveporexton from placebo under the conditions tested. Additionally, in an intravenous self-administration study in rats, oveporexton at 0.03 mg/kg/0.2 mL infusion was self-administered more than vehicle control in cocaine-trained rats, but the other three tested oveporexton doses (0.01, 0.1, and 0.3 mg/kg/0.2 mL infusion) were not self-administered more than vehicle. From this result, HHS concluded that ( printed page 72778) oveporexton produces weak reinforcing effects in male cocaine-maintained rats. 

The human clinical trial data described by HHS further demonstrate oveporexton's abuse potential. In a human abuse potential study, healthy adult non-dependent, recreational drug users with CNS stimulant experience rated all evaluated doses of oveporexton (6 mg, 18 mg, and 30 mg, taken orally) more favorably than placebo across primary and secondary endpoints associated with abuse potential. In this study, the maximal subjective Drug Liking scores (primary endpoint) were not statistically significantly different between the positive control (phentermine 75 mg; schedule IV) and oveporexton (18 mg and 30 mg). In addition, HHS's review of adverse events across clinical safety and efficacy studies indicated that oveporexton produced dose-dependent increases in potential abuse-related treatment-emergent adverse events. The most common oveporexton potential abuse-related adverse event in clinical trial participants without narcolepsy was “euphoric mood.” Such adverse events were infrequent in the intended treatment population (persons with NT1) at recommended therapeutic doses of oveporexton (≤4 mg/day).

In conclusion, the pharmacological effects of oveporexton support that oveporexton has a potential for abuse that is similar to that of the schedule IV stimulant phentermine.

 3. The State of Current Scientific Knowledge Regarding the Drug or Other Substance: Oveporexton, chemically known as N -[(2 S, 3 R)-2-[[3-(3,5-difluorophenyl)-2-fluorophenyl]methyl]-4,4-difluoro-1-(2-hydroxy-2-methylpropanoyl)pyrrolidin-3-yl]ethanesulfonamide, is a new molecular entity that was recently FDA-approved for the treatment of NT1 in adults. This approval indicates that oveporexton has an accepted medical use in treatment in the United States. The recommended dosage of oveporexton for the treatment of NT1 is either 1 mg or 2 mg orally, taken after awakening and then three to five hours later. Following oral administration, oveporexton is rapidly absorbed, highly distributed (including to the CNS), and shows approximately dose-proportional increases in systemic exposure. The mean terminal elimination half-life of oveporexton is 23.2 hours. Oveporexton is primarily excreted in the feces following cytochrome P450 3A4-predominant hepatic metabolism, with unchanged oveporexton identified as the major circulating species in plasma. 

 4. Its History and Current Pattern of Abuse: Consistent with the fact that oveporexton is new to the global market, both FDA and DEA are not aware of any diversion or abuse related to oveporexton. Since real-world data on history and patterns of abuse are lacking, there is no data to assess oveporexton's history and current patterns of abuse. However, nonclinical and clinical studies ( see Factors 1 and 2) support that oveporexton has a potential for abuse similar to that of phentermine (schedule IV). 

 5. The Scope, Duration, and Significance of Abuse: FDA is not aware of any diversion or abuse of oveporexton from its manufacture and distribution associated with legitimate drug research, and oveporexton has not been previously marketed (legally or illegally) in the United States. DEA's NFLIS-Drug database confirms that oveporexton is absent from the United States illicit drug market. Since this is a new molecular entity, evidence of the scope, duration, and significance of abuse of oveporexton is limited. However, the available data ( see Factors 1 and 2) indicate that oveporexton has a potential for abuse similar to that of phentermine (schedule IV), and because of this, it is likely to be abused upon its availability in the market. 

 6. What, if any, Risk There Is to the Public Health: HHS reviewed clinical trial adverse event data to evaluate oveporexton's potential public health risk. Oveporexton produces dose-dependent increases in the incidence of adverse events, including potential abuse-related treatment-emergent adverse events. Potential abuse-related treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 19.4 percent of participants without narcolepsy taking 30-75 mg/day oveporexton. Adverse Events of Special Interest, such as insomnia and frequent urination, occurred in up to 16.7 percent of participants without narcolepsy after a 30 mg single dose of oveporexton. DEA adds that transient insomnia and increased urinary frequency occurred in a majority of participants with NT1 taking recommended therapeutic doses of oveporexton (≤4 mg/day) in the Phase 3 trials. 

 DEA adds that Lammers et al. (2026) [6] performed a secondary analysis of a Phase 2 trial in participants with NT1 (N=112) and determined that oveporexton improved attention, memory, and executive function at 8 weeks. The authors postulated that their findings may be because oveporexton is addressing the pathophysiology of NT1 ( i.e., impaired orexigenic neurotransmission) or may be secondary to improved NT1 symptomatology. DEA notes that studies are needed to confirm if cognitive performance benefits extend outside the NT1 population and if the effects are acute or only present after continual use. Nonetheless, DEA considers oveporexton's potential for cognitive enhancement and performance benefits may increase the attractiveness of the drug for diversion and abuse, thereby contributing to oveporexton's overall risk to public health because cognitive enhancement is a major motivation for prescription stimulant diversion and abuse. 

Furthermore, a drug's abuse potential is a key indicator of its public health risk. Data presented in Factors 1-3 suggest that oveporexton possesses an abuse potential similar to that of phentermine—a schedule IV stimulant. Therefore, all things considered, as oveporexton becomes available for marketing, it is anticipated that it will present a similar public health risk to that of phentermine.

 7. Its Psychic or Physiological Dependence Liability: Psychic (or psychological) dependence is a state similar to addiction and can be inferred through animal self-administration studies, human abuse potential studies, case reports, and epidemiological data. In an intravenous self-administration study in cocaine-trained rats, one (of four) oveporexton doses produced a small, but statistically significant increase in the number of infusions per session compared to vehicle control. In a human abuse potential study conducted in non-dependent, recreational drug users with CNS stimulant experience (N=43), the Take Drug Again scores were similar between phentermine 75 mg and supratherapeutic doses of oveporexton (18 mg and 30 mg). The reinforcing effects of oveporexton in animals and subjective effect scores indicative of reinforcing effects in humans align closely with phentermine rather than stronger stimulants ( i.e., schedule II stimulants), suggesting oveporexton's potential to induce drug-seeking behavior is expected to be correspondingly lower than schedule II stimulants. Taken together, these data indicate that oveporexton is unlikely to cause psychic dependence in humans. 

 Physical dependence develops from physiological adaptation to repeated drug use and manifests as withdrawal ( printed page 72779) symptoms after abrupt drug discontinuation or reduction of a drug. A minority of female rats exhibited some sporadic effects of oveporexton withdrawal (writhing/abdominal spasm, eye closure and jaw chomping) following discontinuation after 28 days of oral oveporexton administration, but there were no robust signals of physical dependence. HHS reviewed drug-discontinuation-emergent adverse events from six repeated-dose oveporexton trials (N=277 participants) to determine if there

# Establishment of the Oval Office National Monument

 A Proclamation 

The Oval Office stands as one of the most recognizable and historically significant spaces in the United States. Since its establishment in its present location and form during the administration of President Franklin D. Roosevelt, it has served as the principal working office of the President of the United States. Decisions of profound national and international consequence have been made within its walls. It has hosted heads of state, shaped the daily conduct of the executive branch, and become a symbol of the American Presidency itself.

The room's distinctive oval design, first introduced in the West Wing under President William Howard Taft and refined in the early 1930s, reflects both practical and ceremonial purposes. Its architecture, finishes of lasting character, and continuous association with the Presidency give the Oval Office exceptional and unique value in illustrating the history of the United States. The Oval Office possesses an unmatched and unique combination of location, design, setting, materials, workmanship, and an association with historical events that are embedded in our national consciousness.

The White House and its grounds are Federal property administered as part of the President's Park by the National Park Service and are already recognized as a National Historic Landmark. Nonetheless, the Oval Office merits specific recognition and protective management as a discrete historic structure of national significance.

WHEREAS, section 320301 of title 54, United States Code (the “Antiquities Act”), authorizes the President, in the President's discretion, to declare by public proclamation historic landmarks, historic and prehistoric structures, and other objects of historic or scientific interest that are situated upon the lands owned or controlled by the Federal Government to be national monuments, and to reserve as a part thereof parcels of land, the limits of which shall be confined to the smallest area compatible with the proper care and management of the objects to be protected;

WHEREAS, it is in the public interest to preserve the Oval Office as a national monument; and

WHEREAS, I find that the boundaries of the Oval Office represent the smallest area compatible with the proper care and management of the objects of historic and scientific interest identified above;

NOW, THEREFORE, I, DONALD J. TRUMP, President of the United States of America, by the authority vested in me by section 320301 of title 54, United States Code, hereby proclaim the Oval Office as the Oval Office National Monument (monument).

 The monument shall consist of the Oval Office itself (Room 110) together with the Outer Oval Office (Rooms 106 and 108) and the Cabinet Room (Room 105). The boundaries of the monument are the smallest area compatible with the proper care and management of the objects of historic interest to be protected. ( printed page 73136) 

The Secretary of the Interior (Secretary), through the National Park Service, shall manage the monument in a manner that protects its historic character, architectural integrity, and association with the Presidency. The Secretary shall:

(1) develop and implement a management plan, in consultation with the White House Office of Administration and other relevant executive departments, agencies, and offices, that prioritizes the preservation of the monument's structural and significant architectural features;

(2) require documentation, review, and consideration of alternatives before any action that would substantially alter or demolish the monument or its essential architectural elements;

(3) ensure that any proposed changes affecting the monument's historic character are evaluated for consistency with its national significance; and

(4) coordinate with the Committee for the Preservation of the White House and other appropriate advisory bodies.

The Secretary is directed to take all necessary steps to implement this proclamation.

Nothing in this proclamation shall be construed to restrict the President's authority to redecorate the monument, select furnishings, or make ordinary operational and security modifications that do not substantially impair the monument's historic structure or architectural character.

Nothing in this proclamation alters existing statutory exemptions applicable to the White House under the National Historic Preservation Act or diminishes the Congress's authority over Federal property.

IN WITNESS WHEREOF, I have hereunto set my hand this fifth day of November, in the year of our Lord two thousand twenty-six, and of the Independence of the United States of America the two hundred and fifty-first.
