###### Department of Health and Human Services

# AGENCY:

National Institutes of Health, HHS.

# ACTION:

Notice of a Modified System of Records.

# SUMMARY:

In accordance with the requirements of the Privacy Act of 1974, as amended, the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) is publishing notice of modifications to an existing system of records maintained by the National Institutes of Health (NIH), “Administration: National Library of Medicine, User Services and Collection Division (NIH Library),” System No. 09-25-0005. The modifications affect the: System name, Routine uses, System location, System manager(s), Purpose of the system, Categories of individuals covered, Categories of records, Retention and disposal, Policies and practices for retrieval, and Record source categories. The changes to the System of Records Notice (SORN) are fully explained in the “Supplementary Information” section of this notice.

# DATES:

The modified system of records is November 12, 2026, subject to a 30-day period in which to comment on the routine uses, described below. Please submit any comments by December 14, 2026.

# ADDRESSES:

 You may submit comments, identified by the Privacy Act SORN No. 09-25-0005, by any of the following methods: Email: privacy@mail.nih.gov. Mail or hand-delivery: NIH Privacy Act Officer, Office of Management Assessment, National Institutes of Health, 6705 Rockledge Drive, Ste. 601, MSC 7901, Bethesda, MD 20892. Comments received will be available for ( printed page 72885) public inspection at this same address from 9:00 a.m. to 3:00 p.m., Monday through Friday, except federal holidays. Please call (301) 496-4606 for an appointment. 

# FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:

General questions about the proposed modified system of records may be submitted to Dustin Close, NIH Privacy Act Officer, Office of Management Assessment, Office of the Director, National Institutes of Health (NIH), 6705 Rockledge Drive, Ste. 601, MSC 7901, Bethesda, MD 20892.

# SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:

The revised SORN published in this notice for system No. 09-25-0005 is in accordance with 5 U.S.C. 552a(e)(4) and (11), and includes the following significant changes:

- The system's name has been changed from Administration: Library Operations and NIH Library User I.D. File to Administration: National Library of Medicine, User Services and Collection Division (NIH Library).
- The System Locations have been updated to remove old locations that no longer exist, update the room number for building 38, and update the name and room number for building 10.
- The System Managers section has been updated to reflect the new names for the System Manager's roles, remove old designations, and update department locations.
- The purpose section has been updated to remove two purposes (previously 2 and 4) that are no longer done by the program or NIH (providing user documentation and managing invoice and billing transactions). The remaining purposes have been re-numbered accordingly and updated to add clarity.
- An additional category of individuals was added to cover authors and other responsible individuals associated with works in the National Library of Medicine (NLM) and NIH Library collections.
- Category types were updated to cover citations and other bibliographic information, while removing record types that are no longer collected (user codes and photographs).
- Record sources were added to cover data that comes from source systems, including the NLM catalog and NIH Library systems and other federal agency systems.
- Routine Use 4 was removed because the NIH Library system no longer provides the function of billing.
- The new Routine Uses 4 and 5 were added in 2018 as an HHS-wide SORN modification and have been explicitly included in this SORN for additional transparency.
- The policies and practices for retention and disposal of records have been updated to remove dated and superseded records retention schedules.

Alfred C. Johnson,

Deputy Director for Management, National Institutes of Health. 

## SYSTEM NAME AND NUMBER:

National Library of Medicine, User Services and Collection Division, and Office of Research Services, Division of Library Services (NIH Library), 09-25-0005.

### SECURITY CLASSIFICATION:

Unclassified.

### SYSTEM LOCATION:

This system of records is an umbrella system comprising separate sets of records located in National Institutes of Health (NIH) facilities in Bethesda, Maryland, or facilities of contractors of the NIH. Write to the appropriate System Manager listed below for list of current contractor locations.

NIH Library, Building 10, Room 1L19A, 10 Center Drive, Bethesda, MD 20892.

National Library of Medicine, Building 38, Room B1E04, 8600 Rockville Pike, Bethesda, MD 20894.

### SYSTEM MANAGER(S):

Management Analyst, Office of Administration, National Library of Medicine, Building 38A, Room B2N12, 8600 Rockville Pike, Bethesda, MD 20894.

Chief, Library Technology Services Branch, Division of Library Services, Office of Research Services, Office of the Director (OD), Building 10, Room 1L19A, 10 Center Drive, Bethesda, MD 20892.

Chief, Collection Branch, National Library of Medicine, Building 38, Room B1E04, 8600 Rockville Pike, Bethesda, MD 20894.

Access Program Manager, Collection Branch, National Library of Medicine, Building 38, Room B1E04, 8600 Rockville Pike, Bethesda, MD 20894.

### AUTHORITY FOR MAINTENANCE OF THE SYSTEM:

42 U.S.C. 286, National Library of Medicine; 42 U.S.C. 241—Research and Investigations Generally (Public Health Service (PHS) Act 401); 42 U.S.C. 282—Director of National Institutes of Health (PHS Act 402); 42 U.S.C. 284—Directors of National Research Institutes (PHS Act 405).

### PURPOSE(S) OF THE SYSTEM:

Records are used within the agency for these purposes:

1. Monitoring library material for circulation to library users (including providing access information to users and library material copying services).

2. Preservation and security of library material to ensure availability for future generations.

### CATEGORIES OF INDIVIDUALS COVERED BY THE SYSTEM:

1. Users of library services.

2. Authors and other responsible individuals associated with works in the NLM and NIH Library collections: individuals whose names or other identifying information appear in the NIH Library and/or the NLM catalogs, archival, or other descriptive records and associated bibliographic or authority files, including authors, contributors, editors, compilers, and other responsible parties associated with works in the collections.

### CATEGORIES OF RECORDS IN THE SYSTEM:

For library users: name, organization, address, phone number, issue date, email address, signature, identification number, primary identifier, and user group code.

For authors and other responsible individuals associated with works in the NLM and NIH Library collections: bibliographic, archival, and descriptive and associated identifying information, including names; standardized name authority forms; variant names; dates; and other cataloging or archival data used for identification, indexing, and disambiguation purposes.

### RECORD SOURCE CATEGORIES:

Individuals, NLM catalog and NIH Library systems, and publicly available bibliographic, archival, and name authority records maintained by federal agencies and other authoritative sources.

### ROUTINE USES OF RECORDS MAINTAINED IN THE SYSTEM, INCLUDING CATEGORIES OF USERS AND PURPOSES OF SUCH USES:

Under the Privacy Act of 1974, as amended, NIH may disclose information about an individual from this system of records to parties outside HHS, without the individual's prior written consent, pursuant to the following routine uses.

1. To a congressional office from the record of an individual in response to an injury from the congressional office made at the request of that individual.

 2. To the Department of Justice (DOJ), or to a court or other tribunal, when (a) HHS, or any component thereof; (b) any HHS employee in his or her official capacity; (c) any HHS employee in his or her individual capacity where the DOJ (or HHS, where it is authorized to do so) has agreed to represent the employee; or (d) the United States or any agency thereof is a party to ( printed page 72886) litigation or has an interest in such litigation, where HHS determines that the litigation is likely to affect HHS or any of its components, and HHS determines that the use of such records by the DOJ, court or other tribunal is relevant and necessary to the litigation and would help in the effective representation of the governmental party, provided, however that in each case, HHS determines that such disclosure is compatible with the purpose for which the records were collected. 

3. To contractors and staff to monitor library material, services, circulation control; to provide user documentation; and to process or refine the records. Recipients are required to maintain Privacy Act safeguards with respect to those records.

4. To appropriate agencies, entities, and persons when (1) HHS suspects or has confirmed that there has been a breach of the system of records; (2) HHS has determined that as a result of the suspected or confirmed breach there is a risk of harm to individuals, HHS (including its information systems, programs, and operations), the federal government, or national security; and (3) the disclosure made to such agencies, entities, and persons is reasonably necessary to assist in connection with HHS's efforts to respond to the suspected or confirmed breach or to prevent, minimize, or remedy such harm.

5. To another federal agency or federal entity, when HHS determines that information from this system of records is reasonably necessary to assist the recipient agency or entity in (1) responding to a suspected or confirmed breach or (2) preventing, minimizing, or remedying the risk of harm to individuals, the recipient agency or entity (including its information systems, programs, and operations), the federal government, or national security, resulting from a suspected or confirmed breach.

### POLICIES AND PRACTICES FOR STORAGE OF RECORDS:

Records are stored on computer tape and disk, paper file cards, and in IT systems.

### POLICIES AND PRACTICES FOR RETRIEVAL OF RECORDS:

Records are retrieved by name, user group code and/or identification number, or other unique identifier assigned to library users. Catalog, archival, and authority records may be retrieved by the name of an author, contributor, or other responsible individual; by title; by subject; by control number or other bibliographic identifier; or by other descriptive metadata elements associated with works or collections maintained by the NIH Library and the NLM.

### POLICIES AND PRACTICES FOR RETENTION AND DISPOSAL OF RECORDS:

Retention Period: DAA-0443-2026-0001: Unscheduled. In accordance with 36 CFR 1225 and 44 U.S.C. Chapter 33, Records are retained indefinitely pending approval of a National Archives and Records Administration (NARA) records schedule. Records must be preserved and may not be destroyed until disposition authority is approved by NARA.

1. Scientific Bibliographic Master Database: Master bibliographic records containing citation data, indexing terms, abstracts, metadata, authority records, persistent identifiers, and related information documenting the agency's scientific information dissemination mission. Permanent. Transfer a copy to NARA when no longer needed for current agency business or according to an approved transfer agreement.

2. Database Change History and Audit Records: Records documenting additions, deletions, corrections, indexing updates, authority control changes, and quality assurance activities affecting master records. Destroy 10 years after superseded or no longer needed for business use.

3. Data Dictionaries and Metadata Specifications: Documentation describing data elements, schemas, indexing standards, controlled vocabularies, relationships, and database structures. Permanent. Transfer with the master database or according to approved transfer instructions.

4. System Documentation: System design records, technical specifications, interfaces, file layouts, user manuals, and system architecture documentation. Destroy 5 years after system retirement or transfer permanent documentation with the master files, as appropriate.

5. Input Source Files: Publisher submissions, data imports, indexing worksheets, and other source records used to create or update bibliographic records. Destroy 5 years after successful verification and incorporation into the master database.

6. Routine Outputs and Reports: Ad hoc reports, extracts, statistical reports, and working copies generated from the database. Destroy when no longer needed for agency business.

7. Backup and Recovery Copies: Backup copies maintained solely for disaster recovery and continuity purposes. Delete when superseded or no longer required for recovery operations.

### ADMINISTRATIVE, TECHNICAL, AND PHYSICAL SAFEGUARDS:

Authorized Users: Employees who maintain records in this system are instructed to grant regular access only to NIH Library staff members who need to verify that NIH Library identification cards have been issued to those library users requesting services such as reference and interlibrary loans. Other one-time and special access by other employees is granted on a need-to-know basis as specifically authorized by the system manager. The contractor maintains a list of personnel having authority to access records to perform their duties.

 Physical Safeguards: The offices housing the cabinets and file drawers for storage of records are locked during all library off-duty hours. During all duty hours offices are attended by employees who maintain the files. The contractor has secured records storage areas which are not left unattended during the working hours and file cabinets which are locked after hours. 

 Procedural Safeguards: Access to the file is strictly controlled by employees who maintain the files. Records may be removed from files only at the request of the system manager or other authorized employees. Access to computerized records is controlled by the use of security codes known only to authorized users. Contractor personnel receive instruction concerning the significance of safeguards under the Privacy Act. 

These practices are in compliance with the standards of Chapter 45-13 of the HHS General Administration Manual, “Safeguarding Records Contained in Systems of Records,” supplementary Chapter PHS hf: 45-13, and the HHS Automated Information Systems Security Program Handbook.

### RECORD ACCESS PROCEDURES:

Same as Notification Procedures. Requesters should also reasonably specify the record contents being sought. Individuals may also request an accounting of disclosures that have been made of their records, if any.

### CONTESTING RECORD PROCEDURES:

 Write to the official at the address specified under Notification Procedures above and reasonably identify the record and specify the information to be contested, the corrective action sought, and the reasons for the correction, along with supporting information to show how the record is inaccurate, incomplete, untimely, or irrelevant. The right to contest records is limited to information that is incomplete, irrelevant, incorrect, or obsolete. ( printed page 72887) 

### NOTIFICATION PROCEDURES:

Write to the System Manager to determine if a record exists. The requester must also verify his or her identity by providing either a notarization of the request or a written certification that the requester is who he or she claims to be and understands that the knowing and willful request for acquisition of a record pertaining to an individual under false pretenses is a criminal offense under the Privacy Act, subject to a five thousand dollar fine.

### EXEMPTIONS PROMULGATED FOR THE SYSTEM:

None.

### HISTORY:

67 FR 60742 at 60744 (Sept. 26, 2002), 83 FR 6591 (Feb. 14, 2018).

# AGENCY:

Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), DOT.

# ACTION:

Final rule.

# SUMMARY:

This rule amends, suspends, or removes Standard Instrument Approach Procedures (SIAPs) and associated Takeoff Minimums and Obstacle Departure Procedures for operations at certain airports. These regulatory actions are needed because of the adoption of new or revised criteria, or because of changes occurring in the National Airspace System, such as the commissioning of new navigational facilities, adding new obstacles, or changing air traffic requirements. These changes are designed to provide for the safe and efficient use of the navigable airspace and to promote safe flight operations under instrument flight rules at the affected airports.

# DATES:

This rule is effective November 12, 2026. The compliance date for each SIAP, associated Takeoff Minimums, and ODP is specified in the amendatory provisions.

The incorporation by reference of certain publications listed in the regulations is approved by the Director of the Federal Register as of November 12, 2026.

# ADDRESSES:

Availability of matter incorporated by reference in the amendment is as follows:

## For Examination

1. U.S. Department of Transportation, Docket Ops-M30, 1200 New Jersey Avenue SE, West Bldg., Ground Floor, Washington, DC, 20590-0001;

2. The FAA Air Traffic Organization Service Area in which the affected airport is located;

3. The office of Aeronautical Information Services, 6500 South MacArthur Blvd., Oklahoma City, OK 73169 or,

4. The National Archives and Records Administration (NARA).

 For information on the availability of this material at NARA, visit www.archives.gov/​federal-register/​cfr/​ibr-locations or email fr.inspection@nara.gov.

## Availability

 All SIAPs and Takeoff Minimums and ODPs are available online free of charge. Visit the National Flight Data Center online at nfdc.faa.gov to register. Additionally, individual SIAP and Takeoff Minimums and ODP copies may be obtained from the FAA Air Traffic Organization Service Area in which the affected airport is located. 

# FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:

Rune Duke, Manager, Standards Section, Flight Procedures and Airspace Group, Aviation Safety, Federal Aviation Administration. Mailing Address: FAA Mike Monroney Aeronautical Center, Flight Procedures and Airspace Group, 6500 South MacArthur Blvd., STB Annex, Bldg. 26, Room 217, Oklahoma City, OK 73099. Telephone (405) 954-1139.

# SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:

 This rule amends 14 CFR part 97 by amending the referenced SIAPs. The complete regulatory description of each SIAP is listed on the appropriate FAA Form 8260, as modified by the National Flight Data Center (NFDC)/Permanent Notice to Airmen (P-NOTAM), and is incorporated by reference under 5 U.S.C. 552(a), 1 CFR part 51, and 14 CFR 97.20. The large number of SIAPs, their complex nature, and the need for a special format make their verbatim publication in the Federal Register expensive and impractical. Further, pilots do not use the regulatory text of the SIAPs, but refer to their graphic depiction on charts printed by publishers of aeronautical materials. Thus, the advantages of incorporation by reference are realized and publication of the complete description of each SIAP contained on FAA form documents is unnecessary. This amendment provides the affected CFR sections, and specifies the SIAPs and Takeoff Minimums and ODPs with their applicable effective dates. This amendment also identifies the airport and its location, the procedure and the amendment number. 

## Availability and Summary of Material Incorporated by Reference

 The material incorporated by reference is publicly available as listed in the ADDRESSES section. 

The material incorporated by reference describes SIAPs, Takeoff Minimums and ODPs as identified in the amendatory language for part 97 of this final rule.

## The Rule

This amendment to 14 CFR part 97 is effective upon publication of each separate SIAP and Takeoff Minimums and ODP as amended in the transmittal. For safety and timeliness of change considerations, this amendment incorporates only specific changes contained for each SIAP and Takeoff Minimums and ODP as modified by FDC permanent NOTAMs.

The SIAPs and Takeoff Minimums and ODPs, as modified by FDC permanent NOTAM, and contained in this amendment are based on criteria contained in the U.S. Standard for Terminal Instrument Procedures (TERPS). In developing these changes to SIAPs and Takeoff Minimums and ODPs, the TERPS criteria were applied only to specific conditions existing at the affected airports. All SIAP amendments in this rule have been previously issued by the FAA in a FDC NOTAM as an emergency action of immediate flight safety relating directly to published aeronautical charts.

The circumstances that created the need for these SIAP and Takeoff Minimums and ODP amendments require making them effective in less than 30 days.

Because of the close and immediate relationship between these SIAPs, Takeoff Minimums and ODPs, and safety in air commerce, I find that notice and public procedure under 5 U.S.C. 553(b) are impracticable and contrary to the public interest and, where applicable, under 5 U.S.C. 553(d), good cause exists for making these SIAPs effective in less than 30 days.

The FAA has determined that this regulation only involves an established body of technical regulations for which frequent and routine amendments are necessary to keep them operationally current. It, therefore—(1) is not a “significant regulatory action” under Executive Order 12866; (2) is not a “significant rule” under DOT regulatory Policies and Procedures (44 FR 11034; February 26, 1979); and (3) does not warrant preparation of a regulatory evaluation as the anticipated impact is so minimal. For the same reason, the FAA certifies that this amendment will not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities under the criteria of the Regulatory Flexibility Act.

# List of Subjects in 14 CFR Part 97

- Airports
- Incorporation by reference
- Navigation (Air)

Issued in Washington, DC. November 6, 2026.

Rune Duke,

## Adoption of the Amendment

# AGENCY:

Office of Personnel Management.

# ACTION:

Notice of extension of suspension of applications for FLTCIP coverage.

# SUMMARY:

The U.S. Office of Personnel Management (OPM) is announcing an extension of the suspension of applications for FLTCIP coverage that came into effect on December 19, 2024.

# DATES:

The extension will begin on December 19, 2026. The suspension period will remain in effect for 24 months from this date.

# FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:

 You may call 1-800-LTC-FEDS (1-800-582-3337) (TTY: 1-800-843-3557) or visit http://www.ltcfeds.gov/​. For purposes of this Federal Register notice only, the contact at OPM is Julia Elam, Supervisory Analyst, at julia.elam@opm.gov or (202) 606-1560. 

# SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:

 OPM is extending the current suspension of applications for coverage in FLTCIP in light of ongoing volatility in long term care costs and a greatly diminished insurance market. The original suspension notice was published at 87 FR 69345 (November 18, 2022) and suspended FLTCIP applications for 24 months, as authorized by 5 CFR 875.110. The suspension was extended through a second notice for an additional 24 months, published at 89 FR 89662 (November 13, 2024). This extension, which will take effect on December 19, 2026, complies with the requirements of § 875.110(d), which requires OPM to issue a Federal Register notice at least 30 days before the end of the suspension period in order to effectuate another suspension not to exceed 24 additional months. As with the current suspension period, no applications for FLTCIP coverage will be accepted during the extension period, and current enrollees may not apply to increase their coverage. The enrollment status or benefit eligibility of current enrollees will not change due to the suspension. For those in a claim status, there is no change to coverage and the claims reimbursement process. 

 OPM has determined that extending the period of suspension of applications for FLTCIP coverage is in the best interest of the Program. Since the current suspension began, the long-term care insurance market has seen ( printed page 73281) continued contraction due to challenges that include ongoing premium instability, such that the market for traditional long term care insurance, and especially group long term care insurance, is essentially non-existent. These market forces continue to undermine the ability to establish benefit offerings with premium rates that reasonably and equitably reflect the cost of the benefits provided, as required under 5 U.S.C. 9003(b)(2). 

 Authority: 5 U.S.C. 9008; Public Law 116-92, 133 Stat. 1198 (5 U.S.C. 8956 note); 5 CFR 875.110. 

## Signing Statement

The Director of OPM, Scott Kupor, reviewed and approved this document and has authorized the undersigned to electronically sign and submit this document to the Office of the Federal Register for publication.

Office of Personnel Management.

Alexys Stanley,

Federal Register Liaison.

# AGENCY:

Government Accountability Office.

# ACTION:

Final rule; technical amendments.

# SUMMARY:

The Government Accountability Office (GAO) is issuing a final rule to amend its Bid Protest Regulations, promulgated in accordance with the Competition in Contracting Act of 1984 (CICA), to make an administrative change by updating citations to the United States Code to reflect amendment and recodification of underlying statutory provisions. The revisions only reflect changes that update an internet address and that update statutory citations to reflect statutory changes, so GAO has determined that the rule is uncontroversial and therefore it is appropriate to issue a final rule.

# DATES:

This rule is effective November 13, 2026.

# FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:

 Edward T. Goldstein (Managing Associate General Counsel, goldsteine@gao.gov). 

# SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:

## Background 

GAO is revising the Bid Protest Regulations as a result of an addition to the statutory bid protest authority in section 326(b)(1) of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2008, Public Law 110-181, 122 Stat. 63 (Jan. 28, 2008); and as the result of a statutory recodification in the William M. (Mac) Thornberry National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2021, Public Law 116-283, 134 Stat. 3388 (Jan. 1, 2021). Subsection (e) of section 1820 of Public Law 116-283 transferred section 2304c of title 10, United States Code to chapter 245 of title 10 and redesignated it as new section 3406 of title 10, among other things. GAO is also updating an internet address. 

## No Comments 

GAO is not subject to the Administrative Procedure Act and accordingly is not required by law to seek comments before issuing a final rule. Additionally, this final rule makes only technical corrections that are uncontroversial, so comments are not invited. 

## Updated Citations and Address 

GAO revises paragraphs (g) and (l) of 4 CFR 21.5 to reflect an addition to its statutory bid protest authority and the redesignation of the cited statutory provision from subsection 2304c(e) to subsection 3406(f) of Title 10 of the United States Code, respectively. GAO also revises the internet address provided in paragraph (f) of 4 CFR 21.0 to reflect the current address. 

# List of Subjects in 4 CFR Part 21 

- Administrative practice and procedure
- Appeals
- Bid protest regulations
- Government contracts

For the reasons set forth in the preamble, the Government Accountability Office amends 4 CFR part 21 as follows:

# PART 21—BID PROTEST REGULATIONS

1. The authority citation for part 21 is revised to read as follows: 

 Authority: 31 U.S.C. 3551-3557. 

2. Amend § 21.0 by revising paragraph (f) to read as follows: 

§ 21.0

 Definitions.

# AGENCY:

U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, Department of the Army, DoD.

# ACTION:

Notice of final deauthorization list.

# SUMMARY:

 The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (Corps) is publishing the final deauthorization list of water resources development projects and separable elements of projects identified for deauthorization in accordance with Section 301 of the Water Resources Development Act (WRDA) of 2020, as amended by Section 1301 of WRDA 2024 (33 U.S.C. 579d-2). The final list was prepared after consideration of the public comments received on the proposed deauthorization list published in the Federal Register on May 21, 2026 (91 FR 29946). The final list has been submitted to the Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure of the House of Representatives and the Committee on Environment and Public Works of the Senate. 

# DATES:

The final deauthorization list and appendix were submitted to Congress on November 13, 2026.

# ADDRESSES:

 The final deauthorization list and appendix are also available at https://www.usace.army.mil/​Missions/​Civil-Works/​Water-Resources-Development-Act/​. Public comments received on the proposed list may be viewed at https://www.regulations.gov under Docket ID No. COE-2026-0034. 

# FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:

 All requests for further information on this notice may be directed to Ms. Sharon Sartor, Corps Headquarters, at 202-761-4495 or WRDA2024@usace.army.mil.

# SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:

Section 301 of WRDA 2020, as amended by Section 1301 of WRDA 2024 (33 U.S.C. 579d-2) directs the Secretary to develop a proposed list of inactive water resources development projects for deauthorization, provide an opportunity for public input on the proposed list, and submit a final list to Congress. The intent is to identify water resources development projects and separable elements of projects that are no longer viable for construction due to: (1) a lack of local support, (2) a lack of available Federal or non-Federal resources, or (3) an authorizing purpose that is no longer relevant or feasible. The process is intended to identify projects for Congress to deauthorize and to allow the continued authorization of projects that remain viable for construction.

Section 301, as amended, provides that the Secretary shall develop a proposed deauthorization list that identifies water resources development projects and separable elements of projects, authorized for construction before June 10, 2014, that meet one of the three criteria listed above. Projects and separable elements on the list are also those that meet one of two criteria: (1) planning, design, or construction was not initiated before January 4, 2025; or (2) planning, design, or construction was initiated before January 4, 2025, but no funds, Federal or non-Federal, were obligated for planning, design, or construction of the project or separable element during the current fiscal year or any of the 10 preceding fiscal years.

The statute directs the Secretary to prepare the final deauthorization list by considering the comments received and revising the proposed list as necessary to respond to them. The Secretary is also directed to include with the final list an appendix that identifies each project or separable element on the proposed list that is not included on the final list and describes the reasons it is not included. The statute further provides that the final list shall not include any project or separable element for which Federal funds for planning, design, or construction were obligated after development of the preliminary list but before submission of the final list to Congress (33 U.S.C. 579d-2(c)(2)).

 The proposed deauthorization list and notice for public comment was published to the Federal Register on May 21, 2026. The public comment period was 90 days, ending on August 19, 2026. The proposed deauthorization list identified 249 projects and separable elements, with an estimated Federal cost to complete of $3,643,281,554. Comments were received through the Federal eRulemaking Portal and by email. ( printed page 73218) 

 A total of 41 public comment submissions were received on the proposed deauthorization list. Comments were considered by the Assistant Secretary of the Army for Civil Works and a final deauthorization list was developed to include an appendix identifying each project or separable element on the proposed deauthorization list that is not included on the final deauthorization list and the reason for its removal. Projects and separable elements were not included on the final deauthorization list where local support and availability of non-Federal resources were demonstrated. While the projects and separable elements in the appendix were removed from the final deauthorization list, they will be included in future iterations of the deauthorization list if Federal or non-Federal funding is not received to advance these projects or separable elements by December 31, 2027. The final deauthorization list contains 206 projects and separable elements, with an estimated Federal cost to complete of $2,465,487,356. The final deauthorization list and appendix can be found at: https://www.usace.army.mil/​Missions/​Civil-Works/​Water-Resources-Development-Act/​.

The final deauthorization list is submitted to Congress. Deauthorization of identified projects and separable elements will require further legislative action by Congress.

 Authority: This notice is required by Section 301 of the Water Resources Development Act of 2020, as amended by 1301 of the Water Resources Development Act of 2024 (33 U.S.C. 579d-2). 

D. Lee Forsgren,

Principal Deputy Assistant Secretary of the Army for Civil Works Performing the Duties of the Assistant Secretary of the Army (Civil Works).

# AGENCY:

Environmental Protection Agency (EPA).

# ACTION:

Final rule.

# SUMMARY:

This regulation establishes tolerances for residues of ethephon in or on fig. Under the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FFDCA), Interregional Research Project Number 4 (IR-4) submitted a petition to EPA requesting that EPA establish a maximum permissible level for residues of this pesticide in or on the identified commodity.

# DATES:

This rule is effective on November 13, 2026. Objections and requests for hearings must be received on or before January 12, 2027, and must be filed in accordance with the instructions provided in 40 CFR part 178 (see also Unit I.C. of this document).

# ADDRESSES:

 The docket for this action, identified by docket identification (ID) number EPA-HQ-OPP-2025-0148, is available at https://www.regulations.gov. Additional information about dockets generally, along with instructions for visiting the docket center in person, is available at https://www.epa.gov/​dockets. 

# FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:

 Charles Smith, Registration Division (7505T), Office of Pesticide Programs, Environmental Protection Agency, 1200 Pennsylvania Ave. NW, Washington, DC 20460-0001; main telephone number: (202) 566-1030; email address: RDFRNotices@epa.gov. 

# SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:

## I. Executive Summary

### A. Does this action apply to me?

You may be potentially affected by this action if you are an agricultural producer, food manufacturer, or pesticide manufacturer. The following list of North American Industrial Classification System (NAICS) codes is not intended to be exhaustive, but rather provides a guide to help readers determine whether this document applies to them.

- Crop production (NAICS code 111).
- Animal production (NAICS code 112).
- Food manufacturing (NAICS code 311).
- Pesticide manufacturing (NAICS code 32532).

 If you have any questions regarding the applicability of this action to a particular entity, consult the person listed under FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT . 

### B. What is EPA's authority for taking this action?

EPA is issuing this rulemaking under section 408 of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FFDCA), 21 U.S.C. 346a. FFDCA section 408(b)(2)(A)(i) allows EPA to establish a tolerance (the legal limit for a pesticide chemical residue in or on a food) only if EPA determines that the tolerance is “safe.” FFDCA section 408(b)(2)(A)(ii) defines “safe” to mean that “there is a reasonable certainty that no harm will result from aggregate exposure to the pesticide chemical residue, including all anticipated dietary exposures and all other exposures for which there is reliable information.” This includes exposure through drinking water and in residential settings but does not include occupational exposure. FFDCA section 408(b)(2)(C) requires EPA to give special consideration to exposure of infants and children to the pesticide chemical residue in establishing a tolerance and to “ensure that there is a reasonable certainty that no harm will result to infants and children from aggregate exposure to the pesticide chemical residue . . .”

### C. How can I file an objection or hearing request?

Under FFDCA section 408(g), 21 U.S.C. 346a(g), any person may file an objection to any aspect of this regulation and may also request a hearing on those objections. If you fail to file an objection to the final rule within the time period specified in the final rule, you will have waived the right to raise any issues resolved in the final rule. You must file your objection or request a hearing on this regulation in accordance with the instructions provided in 40 CFR part 178. To ensure proper receipt by EPA, you must identify docket ID number EPA-HQ-OPP-2025-0148 in the subject line on the first page of your submission. All objections and requests for a hearing must be in writing and must be received by the Hearing Clerk on or before January 12, 2027.

 The EPA's Administrative Law Judges Division (ALJD), in which the Hearing Clerk is housed, urges parties to file and serve documents by electronic means only, notwithstanding any other particular requirements set forth in other procedural rules governing those proceedings. See “Order Urging Electronic Filing and Service,” dated December 3, 2025, which can be found at https://www.epa.gov/​system/​files/​documents/​2025-12/​2025-12-03-order-urging-electronic-filing-and-service.pdf. Although the EPA's regulations require submission via U.S. Mail or hand delivery, the EPA intends to treat submissions filed via electronic means as properly filed submissions; therefore, the EPA believes the preference for submission via electronic means will not be prejudicial. When submitting documents to the ALJD electronically, a person should utilize the OALJ e-filing system at https://yosemite.epa.gov/​oa/​eab/​eab-alj_​upload.nsf. 

 In addition to filing an objection or hearing request with the Hearing Clerk as described in 40 CFR part 178, please submit a copy of the filing (excluding any Confidential Business Information (CBI)) for inclusion in the public docket at https://www.regulations.gov. Follow the online instructions for submitting ( printed page 73169) comments. Do not submit electronically any information you consider to be CBI or other information whose disclosure is restricted by statute. If you wish to include CBI in your request, please follow the applicable instructions at https://www.epa.gov/​dockets/​commenting-epa-dockets#rules and clearly mark the information that you claim to be CBI. Information not marked confidential pursuant to 40 CFR part 2 may be disclosed publicly by EPA without prior notice. 

## II. Petitioned-For Tolerance

 In the Federal Register of December 16, 2025 (90 FR 58181) (FRL-12474-10-OCSPP), EPA issued a document pursuant to FFDCA section 408(d)(3), 21 U.S.C. 346a(d)(3), announcing the filing of a pesticide petition (PP 5E9168) by Interregional Research Project No. 4 (IR-4), North Carolina State University, 1730 Varsity Drive, Venture IV, Suite 2100, Raleigh, NC 27606. The petition requested that 40 CFR 180.300 be amended by establishing tolerances for residues of the fungicide ethephon, in or on fig at 0.02 parts per million (ppm). That document referenced a summary of the petition prepared by IR-4, the petitioner, which is available in the docket, at http://www.regulations.gov. The U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) submitted a comment supporting the use of ethephon as a plant growth regulator for figs. 

## III. Final Tolerance Action

### A. Aggregate Risk Assessment and Determination of Safety

Consistent with FFDCA section 408(b)(2)(D), and the factors specified in FFDCA section 408(b)(2)(D), EPA has reviewed the available scientific data and other relevant information in support of this action. EPA has sufficient data to assess the hazards of and to make a determination on aggregate exposure for ethephon including exposure resulting from the tolerances established by this action. EPA's assessment of exposures and risks associated with ethephon are summarized in this unit.

 In an effort to streamline its publications in the Federal Register , EPA is not reprinting sections that repeat what has been previously published for tolerance rulemakings of the same pesticide chemical or is otherwise publicly available. Where scientific information concerning a particular chemical remains unchanged, the content of those sections would not vary between tolerance rulemaking and/or registration review decisions, EPA considers referral back to those sections as sufficient to provide an explanation of the information EPA considered in making its safety determination for the new rulemaking. 

 EPA has previously published several tolerance rulemakings for ethephon and the more recent “Ethephon Interim Registration Review Decision Case Number 0382” (EPA-HQ-OPP-2010-0098-0034) in which EPA concluded, based on the available information, that there is a reasonable certainty that no harm would result from aggregate exposure to ethephon and established tolerances for residues of that chemical. EPA is incorporating previously published sections from these rulemakings, human health risk assessments, and registration review decisions as described further in this rulemaking, as they remain unchanged. These sections include toxicological profile, toxicological points of departure/levels of concern, exposure assessment, cancer, dietary exposure of drinking water, safety factor for infants and children, aggregate risk and determination of safety, chronic risk, and analytical enforcement methodology. The risk assessment published in support of this rulemaking is “Ethephon. Human Health Risk Assessment for New Section 3 Use on Fig” which is available in docket EPA-HQ-OPP-2025-0148 at https://www.regulations.gov. 

### B. Toxicological Profile

 EPA has evaluated the available toxicity data and considered its validity, completeness, and reliability as well as the relationship of the results of the studies to human risk. EPA has also considered available information concerning the variability of the sensitivities of major identifiable subgroups of consumers, including infants and children. Specific information on the studies received and the nature of the adverse effects caused by ethephon as well as the no observed adverse effect level (NOAEL) and the lowest observed adverse effect level (LOAEL) from the toxicity studies for ethephon are summarized in the “Ethephon: Human Health Risk Assessment for a New Section 3 Use on Fig”, located in docket EPA-HQ-OPP-2025-0148, which can be found at https://www.regulations.gov. 

### C. Toxicological Points of Departure/Levels of Concern

 Once a pesticide's toxicological profile is determined, EPA identifies toxicological points of departure (POD) and levels of concern to use in evaluating the risk posed by human exposure to the pesticide. For hazards that have a threshold below which there is no appreciable risk, the toxicological POD is used as the basis for derivation of reference values for risk assessment. PODs are developed based on a careful analysis of the doses in each toxicological study to determine the dose at which no adverse effects are observed (the NOAEL) and the lowest dose at which adverse effects of concern are identified (the LOAEL). Uncertainty/safety factors are used in conjunction with the POD to calculate a safe exposure level, generally referred to as a population-adjusted dose (PAD) or a reference dose, and a safe margin of exposure (MOE). For non-threshold risks, the Agency assumes that any amount of exposure will lead to some degree of risk. Thus, the Agency estimates risk in terms of the probability of an occurrence of the adverse effect expected in a lifetime. For more information on the general principles EPA uses in risk characterization and a complete description of the risk assessment process, see https://www.epa.gov/​pesticide-science-and-assessing-pesticide-risks/​human-health-risk-pesticides. 

A summary of the toxicological endpoints for ethephon used for human risk assessment is discussed in the document “Ethephon: Human Health Risk Assessment for a New Section 3 Use on Fig”, pages 14-15, available in docket EPA-HQ-OPP-2025-0148.

### D. Exposure Assessment

#### 1. Dietary Exposure From Food and Feed Uses

In evaluating dietary exposure to ethephon, EPA considered exposure under the petitioned-for tolerances as well as all existing ethephon tolerances in 40 CFR 180.300. EPA assessed dietary exposures from ethephon in food as follows:

 i. Acute Exposure. Quantitative acute dietary exposure and risk assessments are performed for a food-use pesticide, if a toxicological study has indicated the possibility of an effect of concern occurring as a result of a 1-day or single exposure. 

 The acute dietary (food and drinking water) assessment for ethephon was conducted using a refined, probabilistic assessment, incorporating the entire distribution of residues from the USDA Pesticide Data Program (PDP) for apples and grapes and residues from field trials for most other commodities. Default processing factors were used for most commodities for which they were available. Adequate processing studies are available for apples, barley, coffee, cottonseed, grapes, pineapple, tomato, ( printed page 73170) sugarcane, and wheat. Empirical processing factors obtained from those studies were used in the acute analyses. The maximum theoretical dietary burdens (MTDB) in beef and dairy cattle, poultry, and swine were previously determined at the time of the Tolerance Reassessment Eligibility Document using the established uses of ethephon. The proposed new use on fig does not include new feedstuff items and does not impact previously calculated MTDBs. MTDBs were calculated based on average or highest average anticipated residues (ARs) from field trial data and a diet comprised of cotton, wheat, and soybean. 

 ii. Chronic Exposure. In conducting the chronic dietary exposure assessment, a refined assessment used average field trial residues, average PDP residues along with tolerance level residues, and average percent crop treated (PCT) estimates where available. Default processing factors were used for most commodities. Adequate processing studies are available for apples, barley, coffee, cottonseed, grapes, pineapple, tomato, sugarcane, and wheat. As a result, empirical processing factors obtained from those studies were used in the chronic analyses. The same ARs were used for livestock commodities as in the acute analyses. As with the acute assessment, where no PCT data were available, the chronic assessment assumed 100 PCT for those commodities. 

 iii. Cancer. Based on the data summarized in “Ethephon: Human Health Risk Assessment for a New Section 3 Use on Fig”, available in docket EPA-HQ-OPP-2025-0148, EPA has concluded that ethephon should be classified as “Not Likely to be Carcinogenic to Humans”. Therefore, a dietary exposure assessment for the purpose of assessing cancer risk is unnecessary. 

 iv. Anticipated Residue and PCT Information. Section 408(b)(2)(E) of FFDCA authorizes EPA to use available data and information on the anticipated residue levels of pesticide residues in food and the actual levels of pesticide residues that have been measured in food. If EPA relies on such information, EPA must require, pursuant to FFDCA section 408(f)(1), that data be provided 5 years after the tolerance is established, modified, or left in effect, demonstrating that the levels in food are not above the levels anticipated. For the present action, EPA will issue such data call-ins as are required by FFDCA section 408(b)(2)(E) and authorized under FFDCA section 408(f)(1). Data will be required to be submitted no later than 5 years from the date of issuance of these tolerances. 

Section 408(b)(2)(F) of FFDCA states that the Agency may use data on the actual percent of food treated for assessing chronic dietary risk only if the following conditions are met.

- Condition a: The data used are reliable and provide a valid basis to show what percentage of the food derived from such crop is likely to contain the pesticide residue. 
- Condition b: The exposure estimate does not underestimate exposure for any significant subpopulation group. 
- Condition c: Data are available on pesticide use and food consumption in a particular area, the exposure estimate does not understate exposure for the population in such area. 

In addition, the Agency must provide for periodic evaluation of any estimates used. To provide for the periodic evaluation of the estimate of PCT as required by FFDCA section 408(b)(2)(F), EPA may require registrants to submit data on PCT.

The following maximum PCT estimates were used in the acute dietary risk assessment for the following crops that are currently registered for ethephon: apples: 25%; barley: 5%; blackberry: 2.5%; blueberry: 5%; cantaloupe: 5%; sweet cherry: 5%; tart cherry: 75%; cotton: 65%; grapes (table): 35%; grape (raisin): 15%; grape juice: 2.5%; grape (/wine): 2.5%; peppers: 5%; tomato: 40%, walnut: 35%, and wheat: 5%. The PCT for cotton was used to refine the anticipated residues for ruminant commodities: 65% for the acute analysis.

The following average PCT estimates were used in the chronic dietary risk assessment for the following crops that are currently registered for ethephon: apples: 15%; barley 5%; cantaloupe: 5%; sweet cherry: 2.5%; tart cherry: 65%; cotton: 50%; grapes (table): 25%; grape (raisin): 5%; grape juice: 2.5%; grape (/wine): <1%; peppers: 5%; tomato: 20%; walnut: 25%.; and wheat 5%. The PCT for cotton was used to refine the anticipated residues for ruminant commodities: 50% for chronic analysis.

In most cases, EPA uses available data from USDA/National Agricultural Statistics Service, proprietary market surveys, and the National Pesticide Use Database for the chemical/crop combination for the most recent 6-7 years. EPA uses an average PCT for chronic dietary risk analysis. The average PCT figure for each existing use is derived by combining available public and private market survey data for that use, averaging across all observations, and rounding to the nearest 5%, except for those situations in which the average PCT is less than one. In those cases, 1% is used as the average PCT and 2.5% is used as the maximum PCT. EPA uses a maximum PCT for acute dietary risk analysis. The maximum PCT figure is the highest observed maximum value reported within the recent 6 years of available public and private market survey data for the existing use and rounded up to the nearest multiple of 5%.

The Agency believes that the three conditions discussed in Unit III.D.1.iv. have been met. With respect to Condition a, PCT estimates are derived from Federal and private market survey data, which are reliable and have a valid basis. The Agency is reasonably certain that the percentage of the food treated is not likely to be an underestimation. As to Conditions b and c, regional consumption information and consumption information for significant subpopulations is taken into account through EPA's computer-based model for evaluating the exposure of significant subpopulations including several regional groups. Use of this consumption information in EPA's risk assessment process ensures that EPA's exposure estimate does not understate exposure for any significant subpopulation group and allows the Agency to be reasonably certain that no regional population is exposed to residue levels higher than those estimated by the Agency. Other than the data available through national food consumption surveys, EPA does not have available reliable information on the regional consumption of food to which ethephon may be applied in a particular area.

#### 2. Dietary Exposure From Drinking Water

 The new use on fig does not result in an increase in the estimated residue levels in drinking water, so EPA used the same estimated drinking water concentrations identified in the 2015 human health risk assessment for registration review of ethephon. All registered uses of ethephon were evaluated with the Surface Water Concentration Calculator and Pesticide Root Zone Model Ground Water to determine the Estimated Drinking Water Concentrations (EDWCs). These models were running using the maximum use patterns to produce drinking water value in surface and groundwater. The surface water EDWCs were higher than the groundwater; as a result, the groundwater EDWCs are not being presented. The surface water EDWC for ethephon is not expected to exceed 25.7 parts per billion for 1-in-10-year acute, ( printed page 73171) and 0.46 for the 1-in-10-year annual average. For the chronic assessment, the EDWC point estimate was incorporated. For acute assessment, the Agency generated daily time series outputs that simulate 30 years of residue of ethephon in surface drinking water using the scenario with the highest 1-in-10-year daily average. 

#### 3. From Non-Dietary Exposure

 The term “residential exposure” is used in this document to refer to non-occupational, non-dietary exposure ( e.g., for lawn and garden pest control, indoor pest control, termiticides, and flea and tick control on pets). 

 Ethephon is currently registered for the following uses that could result in residential exposures: ornamentals, home gardens/trees, and golf course use. All registered ethephon product labels with residential use sites ( e.g., ornamentals and home gardens/trees) require that handlers wear specific clothing ( e.g., long sleeve shirt/long pants) and/or use PPE. Therefore, EPA has made the assumption that these products are not for homeowner use and has not conducted a quantitative residential handler assessment. There is the potential for post-application exposure for individuals exposed as a result of being in an environment that has been previously treated with ethephon ( i.e., ornamentals and home gardens/trees, and golf courses). However, in the absence of a dermal point of departure, dermal post-application exposure assessments were not conducted. The prior post-application incidental oral assessment for children (1 to <2 years old) playing on treated turf is no longer necessary since residential turf was removed from all ethephon product labels. Further information regarding EPA standard assumptions and generic inputs for residential exposures may be found at https://www.epa.gov/​pesticide-science-and-assessing-pesticide-risks/​standard-operating-procedures-residential-pesticide.

#### 4. Cumulative Effects From Substances With a Common Mechanism of Toxicity

Section 408(b)(2)(D)(v) of FFDCA requires that, when considering whether to establish, modify, or revoke a tolerance, the Agency consider “available information” concerning the cumulative effects of a particular pesticide's residues and “other substances that have a common mechanism of toxicity.”

Unlike other pesticides for which EPA has followed a cumulative risk approach based on a common mechanism of toxicity, EPA has not made a common mechanism of toxicity finding as to ethephon and any other substances. For the purposes of this action, therefore, EPA has not assumed that ethephon has a common mechanism of toxicity with other substances.

In 2016, EPA's Office of Pesticide Programs released a guidance document, Pesticide Cumulative Risk Assessment: Framework for Screening Analysis. This document provides guidance on how to screen groups of pesticides for cumulative evaluation using a two-step approach beginning with the evaluation of available toxicological information and if necessary, followed by a risk-based screening approach. This framework supplements the existing guidance documents for establishing common mechanism groups and conducting cumulative risk assessments.

 Ethephon is an organophosphonate ethylene releaser, as opposed to an organophosphate. It is structurally different from and demonstrates different physical and chemical properties than traditional organophosphate

# Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Program and Medicare Prescription Drug Benefit Program 

 A Rule by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services on 11/09/2026
