# AGENCY:

Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS), Health and Human Services (HHS).

# ACTION:

Final rule.

# SUMMARY:

This rule finalizes and codifies the Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Program (“Negotiation Program”) and establishes certain new policies for the Negotiation Program and the Medicare Prescription Drug Benefit Program (“Part D Program”) as required by the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022. This final rule also finalizes a proposed policy for specific fixed combination drugs that are new formulations.

# DATES:

 Effective date: These regulations are effective on December 5, 2026. 

 Applicability date: These regulations are applicable to the Negotiation Program beginning with respect to initial price applicability year 2029 and to Part D Program coverage beginning January 1, 2029. 

# FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:

 Elisabeth Daniel, IRARebateandNegotiation@cms.hhs.gov, or (667) 290-8793, for issues related to the Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Program. 

# SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:

## I. Executive Summary and Background

### A. Executive Summary

#### 1. Purpose

This final rule finalizes and codifies policies related to the implementation of certain provisions of the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 (IRA) (Pub. L. 117-169, August 16, 2022) and amendments made by the “Working Families Tax Cut” legislation (Pub. L. 119-21, July 4, 2025).

This final rule also finalizes and codifies policies for the Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Program at part 429 consistent with sections 1191 through 1198 of the Social Security Act (hereinafter “the Act”) as well as policies for the Medicare Prescription Drug Benefit Program at part 423 consistent with section 11001(b) of the IRA, which made certain amendments to the Act, including with respect to Medicare Part D.

#### 2. Summary of the Provisions

 We are codifying policies established in final guidance for the Negotiation Program [1] in regulatory text. Specifically, we are codifying, with limited modification, the policies set forth in guidance for the Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Program by adding the new part 429 to title 42, Chapter IV of the Code of Federal Regulations and modifying policies for the Medicare Prescription Drug Benefit Program at part 423. 

In addition, we are codifying new policies for the Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Program as follows:

- Finalizing § 429.125(b)(4)(ii) regarding treatment of specific fixed combination drugs in our determinations of qualifying single source drugs. In this section, we are establishing a policy for specific fixed combination drugs that we determine are new formulations of existing drugs. Under this policy, if CMS determines that products with the same New Drug Application (NDA)/Biologics License Application (BLA) holder differ in active moiety(ies), active ingredient(s), or antigen component(s) due to the inclusion of an active moiety, active ingredient, or antigen component that creates a new formulation and enables an alternative route of administration for the co-administered active moiety(ies), active ingredient(s), or antigen component(s), then CMS will identify the potential qualifying single source drug using all dosage forms and strengths of the shared active moiety(ies), active ingredient(s), or antigen component(s) that are offered by the same NDA/BLA holder.
- Finalizing § 429.125(c)(3)(i), to clarify how CMS will identify the day from which to measure the 7- and 11-year time since approval and licensure periods for drugs that formerly qualified for the Orphan Drug Exclusion.
- Finalizing § 429.130, to codify the process and schedule according to which CMS reviews information to determine if the manufacturer of a generic drug or biosimilar that is approved or licensed, respectively, is engaged in Bona Fide Marketing (as defined in § 429.20) of that generic drug or biosimilar.
- Finalizing § 429.210(c), to provide additional details related to the Primary Manufacturer transfer of responsibility for all requirements of the Negotiation Program Agreement to an acquiring entity.
- Finalizing § 429.415(a)(2) and § 429.510(d)(2)(ii), to explain how CMS will calculate the 30-day equivalent supply for a selected drug or therapeutic alternative, respectively, payable under Part B that is typically administered one time (for example, some vaccines, gene therapies, and cancer therapies).
- Finalizing § 429.440 with modifications, to explain how CMS will implement the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs for initial price applicability years 2029 and 2030. We are modifying our proposed stepwise approach, at § 429.440(b)(4), for calculating a selected drug's ceiling in the event that certain ceiling amounts are below the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs.
- Finalizing §§ 429.605 and 429.610 with modifications, to clarify when off-label use would be considered for renegotiation eligibility and selection by aligning the renegotiation eligibility and selection policies for off-label use with the initial offer development process.

 Unless otherwise specified, CMS finalizes that the provisions herein would apply with respect to all initial price applicability years beginning with initial price applicability year 2029, including, for example, with respect to the selection of drugs and the negotiation or renegotiation of MFPs for initial price applicability year 2029 that will take place during calendar year 2027. In this final rule, unless otherwise specified, references hereinafter to “the Negotiation Program Guidance” are to the most recent program guidance published by CMS, which is the Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Program: Final Guidance, Implementation of sections 1191-1198 of the Act for Initial Price Applicability Year 2028 and Manufacturer Effectuation of the Maximum Fair Price in 2026, 2027, and 2028 that was published on September 30, 2025. In this final rule, unless otherwise specified, references hereinafter to “the revised guidance for initial price applicability year 2026” are to the Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Program: Revised Guidance, Implementation of Sections 1191-1198 of the Social Security Act for Initial Price Applicability Year 2026 that was published by CMS on June 30, 2023. Additionally, in this final rule, unless otherwise specified, references ( printed page 72177) hereinafter to “the final guidance for initial price applicability year 2027” are to the Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Program: Final Guidance, Implementation of Sections 1191-1198 of the Social Security Act for Initial Price Applicability Year 2027 and Manufacturer Effectuation of the Maximum Fair Price in 2026 and 2027 that was published by CMS on October 2, 2024. 

Given that the identification and selection of drugs for negotiation and renegotiation occurs more than 2 years before the first application of the MFP (that is, before the start of the selected drug's first initial price applicability year), the processes for drugs that were selected for negotiation for initial price applicability years 2026, 2027, and 2028 and for renegotiation for initial price applicability year 2028 will be at varying stages of implementation when this rule is finalized. Consistent with the program instruction requirement at sections 11001(c) and 11002(c) of the IRA, the program guidance issued by CMS for initial price applicability years 2026, 2027, and 2028 remains applicable and is not superseded by this final rule with respect to such years. In other words, because sections 11001(c) and 11002(c) of the IRA require CMS to implement the Negotiation Program for initial price applicability years 2026, 2027, and 2028 through program instruction and other forms of program guidance, the requirements for a selected drug that was included on the list of selected drugs with respect to initial price applicability year 2026, 2027, or 2028 are set forth with respect to such years in the applicable program guidance. Revisions to the implementation of policy for 2026, 2027, and 2028 with respect to drugs selected for initial price applicability years 2026, 2027, and 2028 would be addressed by CMS through publication of revised guidance. In accordance with the expiration of the statutory program instruction requirement at the end of 2028, CMS finalizes that the provisions herein, as applicable, will apply starting in 2029 with respect to the drugs selected for initial price applicability years of 2026, 2027, or 2028.

Finally, CMS reminds interested parties that the exclusion for small biotech drugs from what is otherwise a negotiation-eligible drug under section 1192(d)(2) of the Act ended in initial price applicability year 2028 and is, therefore, not codified in this final rule. However, the definition of an eligible small biotech drug for purposes of the calculation of the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs on the maximum fair price for small biotech drugs under section 1194(d) of the Act is included in this final rule (as described in more detail in section II.E.2. of this final rule).

#### 3. Summary of Costs and Benefits

We are finalizing new policies for the Negotiation Program as follows: a policy for specific fixed combination drugs that are new formulations; clarification for drugs that formerly qualified for the orphan drug exclusion; revisions regarding process and schedule of CMS review of information in making the determination for Bona Fide Marketing; additional details related to the Primary Manufacturer transfer of responsibility for all requirements of the Negotiation Program Agreement to an acquiring entity; calculation of the 30-day equivalent supply for a selected drug that is typically administered one time; implementation of the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs for initial price applicability years 2029 and 2030; and clarification of off-label use in consideration for renegotiation eligibility and selection. In summary, the effects of the IRA are to reduce government expenditures for Part B, to increase expenditures for Part D through 2030, and to decrease Part D expenditures beginning in 2031. For a detailed discussion of the economic impacts, see section VI. of this final rule.

### B. Background

Sections 11001 and 11002 of the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 (IRA) (Pub. L. 117-169), signed into law on August 16, 2022, establish the Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Program (hereinafter the “Negotiation Program”) to negotiate maximum fair prices (MFPs) for certain high expenditure, single source drugs and biological products. Specifically, in accordance with section 1191(c)(3) of the Act, MFP means, with respect to a year during a price applicability period and with respect to a selected drug (as defined in section 1192(c) of the Act) with respect to such period, the price negotiated pursuant to section 1194 of the Act, and updated pursuant to section 1195(b) of the Act, as applicable, for such drug and year. The requirements for this program are described in sections 1191 through 1198 of the Act, as added by sections 11001 and 11002 of the IRA and as amended by section 71203 of the “Working Families Tax Cut” legislation (Pub. L. 119-21).

Under the IRA, with respect to each initial price applicability year, CMS shall: (1) publish a list of selected drugs in accordance with section 1192 of the Act; (2) enter into agreements with manufacturers of selected drugs in accordance with section 1193 of the Act; (3) negotiate MFPs for such selected drugs in accordance with section 1194 of the Act; (4) publish MFPs for selected drugs in accordance with section 1195 of the Act; (5) carry out administrative duties and compliance monitoring in accordance with section 1196 of the Act; and (6) impose civil monetary penalties (CMPs) in accordance with section 1197 of the Act. With respect to initial price applicability year 2028 and subsequent years, in accordance with section 1194(f) of the Act, CMS shall also: (1) determine renegotiation-eligible drugs; (2) determine whether to select drugs for renegotiation; and (3) renegotiate the MFP for any drug selected for renegotiation. To the extent applicable, any references in this final rule to the “MFP” include a renegotiated MFP. Section 1198 of the Act establishes certain limitations on administrative and judicial review relevant to the Negotiation Program.

Additionally, on July 4, 2025, the “Working Families Tax Cut” legislation was signed into law. Section 71203(a)(2) of the “Working Families Tax Cut” legislation amended section 1192(e)(3)(A) of the Act to modify the requirements for a drug to qualify for the Orphan Drug Exclusion. Section 71203(a)(3) of the “Working Families Tax Cut” legislation also added new section 1192(e)(4) of the Act, which describes the treatment of former orphan drugs.

 For the first year of the Negotiation Program, the Secretary of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (“the Secretary”) selected 10 high expenditure, single source drugs covered under Part D for negotiation. The negotiated MFPs for these drugs took effect in initial price applicability year 2026. [2] The Secretary selected an additional 15 drugs covered under Part D for negotiation for initial price applicability year 2027, [3] and 15 drugs covered under Part D or payable under Part B or both for initial price applicability year 2028. [4] The Secretary will select up to 20 drugs covered under Part D or payable under Part B or both for initial price applicability year 2029 and subsequent initial price applicability years. Beginning with initial price applicability year 2028, the Secretary could also select drugs from initial price applicability year 2026 and ( printed page 72178) subsequent initial price applicability years for renegotiation. The Secretary selected one drug for renegotiation for initial price applicability year 2028. [5] 

 For initial price applicability years 2026 through 2028 of the Negotiation Program, sections 11001(c) and 11002(c) of the IRA direct CMS to implement the Negotiation Program through program instruction and other forms of program guidance. CMS issued initial or draft versions of program guidance for each initial price applicability year 2026, [6] 2027, [7] and 2028 [8] and requested public comment on each version. CMS then issued a revised or final version of the guidance for each of these program years. [9 10 11] In the final rule, we proposed to codify these requirements at parts 423 and 429 to title 42, chapter IV of the Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) to implement sections 11001 and 11002 of the IRA. The effective date of the finalized provisions is discussed in section I.A.5. of this final rule. 

Consistent with the program instruction requirement of sections 11001(c) and 11002(c) of the IRA, CMS will issue program guidance related to manufacturer effectuation of the MFP for 2028, including with respect to drugs payable under Part B. CMS intends to codify requirements related to MFP effectuation for 2029 and subsequent years in future rulemaking. CMS stated in the Negotiation Program Guidance its intent to codify MFP effectuation policies for 2029 and subsequent years after guidance for 2028 has been finalized.

### C. Publication of the Proposed Rule and General, Out-of-Scope, and Within Scope Public Comments

#### 1. Publication of the Proposed Rule

In response to the Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Program and Medicare Prescription Drug Benefit Program proposed rule (91 FR 36236 through 36368) (“proposed rule”), we received approximately 11,330 timely comment letters containing a variety of feedback and recommendations on the proposed rule and the information collection requests (ICRs) contained within the proposed rule.

#### 2. General Comments

We received general comments on the Negotiation Program proposed rule. The following is a summary of the general comments we received and our responses.

 Comment: Many commenters expressed general support for the Negotiation Program and the proposed policies. 

 Response: We thank commenters for their support. 

 Comment: Some commenters expressed general opposition to the Negotiation Program and the proposed policies. 

 Response: We appreciate the commenters for sharing their concern. 

 Comment: Some commenters noted that codifying policies of the Negotiation Program in regulation should not be an opportunity for CMS to expand the program requirements. A commenter urged CMS to assess whether proposed policies are consistent with statute, supported by reasoned decision making, and responsive to stakeholder comments as it implements the Negotiation Program. 

 Response: We appreciate this input and note that we have pursued implementation in accordance with the statutory requirements of the Negotiation Program. We appreciate the comments received from interested parties on the proposed rule. We read and responded to all significant comments received timely. 

 Comment: Many commenters expressed concern about the impact of the Negotiation Program on innovation and drug development, as well as concern about creating uncertainty in the pharmaceutical market. A few commenters recommended CMS continue to be transparent as it implements the Negotiation Program, and one of these commenters noted that CMS should adopt clear standards, consistent definitions, and predictable procedures across the Negotiation Program. A couple of commenters recommended CMS monitor and report on the impact of the Negotiation Program on patient access to prescription drugs. 

 Response: We thank these commenters for their input. Although the U.S. prescription drug market is the largest in the world—with a track record of fostering innovation—patients in the United States generally pay more for prescription drugs than anywhere else. [12] We believe the Negotiation Program will make prescription drugs more affordable for people with Medicare and the Medicare program—without restricting innovation and new product research and development. [13 14] We also expect the Negotiation Program to encourage drug manufacturers to create business models to stay competitive, fostering the development of new treatments. Only drugs that have been approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for at least 7 years and only biological products that have been licensed by the FDA for at least 11 years are eligible for selection as part of the Negotiation Program, unless they are otherwise excluded in accordance with statute. With the implementation of the Negotiation Program, we believe prescription drugs will be more affordable, allowing more patients to purchase those prescription drugs and adhere to their medications. As a result, prescription drug sales likely will continue to grow and drug manufacturers will reap the rewards of more patients being able to afford their medications. 

#### 3. Out of Scope Comments

Many comments, including those related to implementation of policies and processes of maximum fair price (MFP) effectuation, such as operations of the Medicare Transaction Facilitator (“MTF”), were out of scope for purposes of this rulemaking.

#### 4. Within Scope Comments

 Summaries of the public comments within the scope of the proposed rule and our responses to those public comments are provided in the various sections of this final rule under the appropriate heading. Commenters included drug manufacturers and their trade associations, patient advocacy organizations, thought leaders, pharmacies and their trade associations, health plans, pharmacy benefit managers and their trade association, ( printed page 72179) and individuals. A summary of the major issues and our responses follow. 

### D. Waiver of Delay in Effective Date

 The Congressional Review Act (CRA) generally requires that the effective date of a major rule be 60 days after the rule is published in the Federal Register . 5 U.S.C. 801(a)(3)(A)(ii). The CRA allows an agency to issue a rule that would otherwise be subject to a 60-day delayed effective date requirement with an effective date at such time as the Federal agency promulgating the rule determines in circumstances where notice and public procedure are impractical, unnecessary, or contrary to the public interest (5 U.S.C. 808(2)). 

 CMS is waiving the 60-day delay in the effective date for this rule to allow it to meet the statutory deadline of February 1 for publication of the selected drug list (as required by sections 1192(a) and 1191(b)(3) of the Act), and avoid an infeasible scenario where CMS must wait until 60 days after the date the rule is published in the Federal Register to close the collection of Initial Delay Requests from Biosimilar Manufacturers (CMS-10844, OMB 0938-1452, Expiration 11/30/2028) as we are finalizing in § 429.110. To meet the statutory deadline of February 1 for publication of the selected drug list (as required by sections 1192(a) and 1191(b)(3) of the Act), based on experience from initial price applicability years 2026, 2027, and 2028, CMS needs a minimum of approximately seven weeks to conduct the review process for Initial Delay Requests, as specified in section 1192(f) of the Act. The volume of Initial Delay Requests we receive varies by year, as well as the scope and complexity of review, since each application presents unique drug-specific considerations. Collecting and reviewing Initial Delay Requests in January 2027 without a waiver of the 60-day delay in the effective date would be infeasible for CMS to make determinations with respect to such requests, as CMS would have insufficient time to: (1) review such request(s); (2) request additional information and documents from the Biosimilar Manufacturer necessary to make determinations (if applicable); (3) allow a Biosimilar Manufacturer time to produce and submit to CMS the requested information (consistent with section 1192(f)(1)(B)(ii)(II) of the Act); and (4) review the additional information and documents submitted by Biosimilar Manufacturers to determine whether the selection of a negotiation-eligible drug that includes the reference product for the Biosimilar should be delayed, before the statutory deadline of February 1 for publication of the selected drug list (as required by sections 1192(a) and 1191(b)(3) of the Act). 

Review of an Initial Delay Request may require CMS to consider a substantial volume of technical information, and potentially request additional information from the Biosimilar Manufacturer, in order to make a determination. For example, in reviewing an Initial Delay Request pursuant to section 1192(f) of the Act, CMS must, among other actions, determine whether there is a high likelihood that the Biosimilar Manufacturer's Biosimilar will be licensed and marketed under section 351(k) of the Public Health Service Act before the date that is 2 years after the selected drug publication date with respect to such initial price applicability year for which a reference drug would be included on the selected drug list absent a successful Initial Delay Request (the High Likelihood Deadline). CMS must also, among other actions, determine that the Biosimilar Manufacturer and the Reference Manufacturer have not entered into an agreement that (1) requires or incentivizes the Biosimilar Manufacturer to submit an Initial Delay Request or (2) directly or indirectly restricts the quantity of the Biosimilar that may be sold in the United States over a specified period of time.

As part of the Initial Delay Request, the Biosimilar Manufacturer must submit all agreements related to the Biosimilar filed with the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) or the Assistant Attorney General pursuant to subsections (a) and (c) of section 1112 of the Medicare Prescription Drug, Improvement, and Modernization Act of 2003, and to the extent available, the manufacturing schedule for the Biosimilar submitted to FDA during its review of the application for licensure and the Biosimilar Manufacturer's disclosures pertaining to the marketing of the Biosimilar (for example, in filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission required under section 12(b), 12(g), 13(a), or 15(d) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 or comparable documentation distributed to the shareholders of privately held companies) about capital investment, revenue expectations, and other actions typically taken by a manufacturer in the normal course of business in the year (or the 2 years, as applicable) before marketing of a Biosimilar.

In this example, CMS must review the aforementioned materials to determine whether there is a high likelihood that the Biosimilar will be licensed and marketed before the High Likelihood Deadline and whether there are any agreements between the Biosimilar Manufacturer and Reference Manufacturer that would require the denial of the Initial Delay Request. If CMS began reviewing Initial Delay Requests in January 2027, CMS would have insufficient time for the following actions before the February 1 statutory publication deadline for the selected drug list. First, CMS must review the applicable agreements filed with the FTC or the Assistant Attorney General, any manufacturing schedule for the Biosimilar submitted to the FDA, and applicable disclosures pertaining to the marketing of the Biosimilar. Second, CMS may need to submit follow up requests to Biosimilar Manufacturers where, for example, the information and documents provided are insufficient for determining whether any agreement(s) violate the statutory requirements for granting the Initial Delay Requests, or where the information and documents provided do not establish clear and convincing evidence as required by statute that the Biosimilar will be marketed before the High Likelihood Deadline. Third, CMS would need to provide the Biosimilar Manufacturer with adequate time to produce and submit to CMS additional information and documents regarding the agreements and marketing of the Biosimilar before the High Likelihood Deadline. Fourth, CMS must review this additional information and documents provided by the Biosimilar Manufacturer to determine if the agreements violate the statutory requirements for granting the Initial Delay Request, and whether there is clear and convincing evidence that the Biosimilar will be marketed before the High Likelihood Deadline. These determinations must be made before the February 1 statutory publication deadline for the selected drug list.

In this example, CMS believes that completing these actions as part of the review of Initial Delay Requests to determine whether the selection of a negotiation-eligible drug should be delayed by one year before the February 1 statutory publication deadline for the selected drug list would be infeasible if CMS began reviewing Initial Delay Requests in January 2027.

 In recognition of these timing requirements, such requests must be due by a date specified by CMS, which would be no later than the end of December of the calendar year prior to the selected drug publication date. A 60-day delay for completion of data collection, after the date of publication ( printed page 72180) in the Federal Register , would be in direct conflict with this provision. 

 Specifically, a 60-day delay in effective date following publication in the Federal Register would mean these actions would not begin until the effective date in early January 2027. This would prevent CMS from reviewing, following up, and granting Initial Delay Requests, if applicable, in accordance with section 1192(f) of the Act by the selected drug publication date for initial price applicability year 2029. Further, a 60-day delay would be inconsistent with our regulation as codified in § 429.110(f). 

 If CMS were to begin reviewing Initial Delay Requests 60 days after the publication of this Final Rule in the Federal Register , CMS would have a period of less than one month to review such requests, which is approximately half the minimum time that CMS believes is necessary, before the February 1 deadline for publication of the selected drug list (as required by sections 1192(a) and 1191(b)(3) of the Act). # AGENCY:

Environmental Protection Agency.

# ACTION:

Final rule.

# SUMMARY:

The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is finalizing amendments to the national emission standards for hazardous air pollutants (NESHAP) for the Polyvinyl Chloride (PVC) and Copolymer Production source category (“PVC NESHAP”) under Clean Air Act (CAA) section 112. For new major sources, the EPA is finalizing the removal of the total non-vinyl chloride organic hazardous air pollutant (HAP) process wastewater emission limit and the associated testing, monitoring, recordkeeping, and reporting requirements. The EPA is also finalizing that the new major source vinyl chloride emission limit acts as a surrogate for non-vinyl chloride organic HAP emissions from process wastewater. The EPA is not taking final action on other aspects of the reconsideration proposal at this time.

# DATES:

This final rule is effective on November 9, 2026.

# ADDRESSES:

 The EPA established a docket for this action under Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OAR-2002-0037. The docket lists all documents at https://www.regulations.gov. Although listed, some information is not publicly available, e.g., Confidential Business Information (CBI) or other information whose disclosure is restricted by statute. The EPA does not place certain other material, such as copyrighted material, on the internet; this material is publicly available only as portable document format versions accessible only on EPA computers in the docket office reading room. The public cannot download certain databases and physical items from the docket but may request these items by contacting the docket office at (202) 566-1744. The docket office has 10 business days to respond to such requests. With the exception of such material, publicly available docket materials are available electronically at https://www.regulations.gov or on EPA computers in the docket office reading room at the EPA Docket Center, WJC West Building, Room Number 3334, 1301 Constitution Ave. NW, Washington, DC. The Public Reading Room hours of operation are 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Eastern Time (ET), Monday through Friday (except Federal holidays). The telephone number for the Public Reading Room is (202) 566-1744, and the telephone number for the EPA Docket Center is (202) 566-1742.

## I. General Information

### A. Executive Summary

 On April 17, 2012, the EPA codified standards for the PVC and Copolymer Production source category at 40 Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) part 63, subpart HHHHHHH (“2012 Final Rule”). [1] Subsequently, industry ( printed page 70797) stakeholders notified the EPA that the Agency used data from outside the PVC and Copolymer Production source category to set the total non-vinyl chloride organic HAP process wastewater emission limits for new major sources and new and existing area sources. The EPA agreed with stakeholders, and in February 2015, the Agency issued a direct final rule to rescind the total non-vinyl chloride organic HAP process wastewater emission limits for new and existing PVC and copolymer production area sources (“2015 Final Rule”). [2] 

 On November 9, 2020, the EPA proposed reconsideration (“2020 Proposal”) of several aspects of the PVC NESHAP in response to petitions for reconsideration on the 2012 Final Rule. [3] As part of that action, the EPA proposed to remove the new and existing major source total non-vinyl chloride organic HAP process wastewater emission limits and the associated testing, monitoring, recordkeeping, and reporting requirements. In addition, the EPA proposed that vinyl chloride can act as a surrogate for non-vinyl chloride organic HAP in PVC and copolymer production process wastewater. This action finalizes the removal of the total non-vinyl chloride organic HAP process wastewater emission limit for new major PVC and copolymer production sources and associated testing, monitoring, recordkeeping, and reporting requirements and finalizes the proposed surrogacy. 

This action will have no immediate cost or emissions impacts as it does not affect existing sources, and the EPA is unaware of any new sources currently subject to the rule. If a new major source PVC and copolymer production facility becomes operational in the future, the EPA estimates that this action will save the facility approximately $2,900 in capital/startup costs and $30,000 in annual costs (in 2025 dollars) due to the reduction in total non-vinyl chloride organic HAP testing, monitoring, recordkeeping, and reporting burdens.

### B. Does this action apply to me?

 Regulated entities. This final action addresses the PVC and Copolymer Production source category regulated under 40 CFR part 63, subpart HHHHHHH. Table 1 of this preamble lists the NESHAP and the associated regulated industrial source category that this action may affect. 

Table 1—NESHAP and Industrial Source Category Affected by This Final Action

| NESHAP | Source category | NAICS a code |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 40 CFR part 63, subpart HHHHHHH | PVC and Copolymer Production | 325211 |
| a North American Industry Classification System (NAICS). | | |

The EPA provides table 1 of this preamble as a guide, not an exhaustive list, of entities that this final rule likely affects for the listed source category. This final rule does not affect Federal, State, local, or Tribal government entities.

 To determine whether this action affects your facility, examine the applicability criteria of this NESHAP. If you have any questions regarding the applicability of this NESHAP, contact the appropriate person listed in the FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT section of this preamble. 

### C. What is the statutory authority for this action?

 CAA section 112, as amended, provides the statutory authority for this action. [4] CAA section 112 establishes a multi-stage regulatory process to develop standards for emissions of HAP from stationary sources. Generally, the first stage involves establishing technology-based standards that reflect application of the maximum achievable control technology (MACT) or appropriate alternative. [5] The second stage involves evaluating those standards within 8 years under CAA section 112(f)(2) to determine whether the EPA needs to promulgate standards to address any remaining risk associated with HAP emissions. [6] This second stage is commonly referred to as the “residual risk review.” In addition to conducting the residual risk review, pursuant to CAA section 112(d)(6), the EPA must review the standards every 8 years and to “revise [them] as necessary,” taking into account any “developments in practices, processes, and control technologies.” [7] This review is commonly referred to as the “technology review.” 

 In the first stage of the CAA section 112 standard-setting process, the EPA promulgates technology-based standards under CAA section 112(d) for categories of sources identified as emitting one or more of the HAP listed in CAA section 112(b). The CAA refers to sources of HAP emissions as either major sources or area sources. “Major sources” are those that emit or have the potential to emit 10 tons per year (tpy) or more of a single HAP or 25 tpy or more of any combination of HAP. [8] All other sources are “area sources.” CAA section 112 establishes different requirements for major source standards and area source standards. For major sources, CAA section 112(d)(2) provides that the technology-based NESHAP must reflect the maximum degree of reduction in emissions of HAP achievable (after considering cost, energy requirements, and non-air quality health and environmental impacts). These standards are commonly referred to as MACT standards. In developing MACT standards, CAA section 112(d)(2) directs the EPA to consider the application of measures, processes, methods, systems, or techniques, including, but not limited to, those that reduce the volume of or eliminate HAP emissions through process changes, substitution of materials, or other modifications; enclose systems or processes to eliminate emissions; collect, capture, or treat HAP when released from a process, stack, storage, or fugitive emissions point; are design, equipment, work practice, or operational standards; or any combination of the above. 

 CAA section 112(d)(3) establishes a minimum control level for MACT standards, known as the MACT “floor,” based on emission controls achieved in practice by the best performing sources. For new sources, the MACT floor cannot be less stringent than the emission control achieved in practice by the best-controlled similar source. For existing sources, the MACT standards can be less stringent than floors for new sources, but the standards cannot be less stringent than the average emission limitation achieved by the best-performing 12 percent of existing sources in the category or subcategory (or the best-performing five sources for categories or subcategories with fewer ( printed page 70798) than 30 sources). [9] In certain instances, as provided in CAA section 112(h), the EPA may set work practice standards in lieu of numerical emission standards. The EPA must also consider control options that are more stringent than the floor, often referred to as “beyond-the-floor” standards, and may establish standards more stringent than the floor taking into consideration the cost of achieving the emission reductions, and any non-air quality health and environmental impacts and energy requirements. [10] 

 In the second stage of the regulatory process, for categories of major sources and any area source categories subject to MACT standards, CAA section 112 requires the EPA to identify and address any remaining ( i.e., “residual”) risk within 8 years pursuant to CAA section 112(f)(2) and to conduct a technology review pursuant to CAA section 112(d)(6). This latter provision requires the EPA to review the technology-based standards and revise them “as necessary (taking into account developments in practices, processes, and control technologies)” no less frequently than every 8 years. In conducting the technology review, the EPA is not required to recalculate the MACT floors that the Agency established in earlier rulemakings. [11] The EPA may consider cost in deciding whether to revise the standards pursuant to CAA section 112(d)(6). [12] Finally, the EPA reviews available data to determine if there are certain unregulated emissions of HAP within the major source category and evaluates these data for use in developing new emission standards. [13] 

For the residual risk review required by CAA section 112(f), within 8 years of promulgating the technology-based standards for a source category, the EPA must evaluate the risk to public health remaining after the application of the technology-based standards and revise the standards, if necessary, to provide an ample margin of safety to protect public health or to prevent an adverse environmental effect, taking into consideration costs, energy, safety, and other relevant factors. For categories of area sources subject to generally available control technologies or management practices (GACT) standards, the CAA does not require the EPA to address residual risk. However, CAA section 112(d)(6) requires the EPA to conduct a technology review for all standards established under CAA section 112(d), including GACT standards that apply to area sources. For categories of area sources subject to GACT standards, CAA section 112(d)(5) and (f)(5) provide that the EPA is not required to conduct a residual risk review under CAA section 112(f)(2).

 The EPA first set MACT standards for the PVC and Copolymer Production major source category in 2002 (“2002 Final Rule”). [14] Upon vacatur and remand by the United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit (“D.C. Circuit”), [15] the EPA promulgated new MACT standards for the PVC and Copolymer Production source category for major sources and revised the area source NESHAP in the 2012 Final Rule. [16] After receiving petitions for reconsideration of the 2012 Final Rule, the EPA proposed reconsideration of several aspects of that rule in the 2020 Proposal. [17] This final action addresses only the proposed reconsideration of the new major source total non-vinyl chloride organic HAP process wastewater emission limit. The EPA intends to address the remaining issues presented in the 2020 Proposal in a separate action. 

### D. Where can I get a copy of this document and other related information?

 In addition to placing this action in the docket, the EPA provides an electronic copy on the internet. Following signature by the EPA Administrator, the Agency will post a copy of this action at https://www.epa.gov/​stationary-sources-air-pollution/​polyvinyl-chloride-and-copolymers-production-national-emission. Following publication in the Federal Register (FR), the EPA will post the Federal Register version of the final rule and key technical documents at this same website. The EPA has placed in the docket a memorandum showing the “track changes” version of the regulatory language that incorporates the changes in this action. [18] 

### E. Judicial Review and Administrative Reconsideration

Under CAA section 307(b)(1), a party may obtain judicial review of this action only by filing a petition for review in the D.C. Circuit by January 8, 2027. CAA section 307(b)(2) prohibits a party from separately challenging this final rule in any civil or criminal enforcement proceedings that the EPA brings.

 CAA section 307(d)(7)(B) provides that, during judicial review, a party may raise only an objection to a rule or procedure that the party raised with reasonable specificity during the period for public comment (including any public hearing). This section also requires the EPA to reconsider the rule if the person raising an objection demonstrates to the Administrator that either it was impracticable to raise the objection during the period for public comment or that the grounds for the objection arose after the period for public comment (but within the time specified for judicial review) and if the objection is of central relevance to the outcome of the rule. Any person seeking to make such a demonstration should submit a petition for reconsideration to the Office of the Administrator, U.S. EPA, Room 3000, WJC South Building, 1200 Pennsylvania Ave. NW, Washington, DC 20460. The person should also send a copy to both the person(s) listed in the FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT section of this preamble, and the Associate General Counsel for the Air and Radiation Law Office, Office of General Counsel (Mail Code 2344A), U.S. EPA, 1200 Pennsylvania Ave. NW, Washington, DC 20460. 

## II. Background

### A. What is the PVC and Copolymer Production source category, and how does the NESHAP regulate HAP emissions from the source category?

 The EPA first promulgated the PVC and Copolymer Production source category NESHAP with the 2002 Final Rule and codified the NESHAP at 40 CFR part 63, subpart J. [19] Following judicial review, the D.C. Circuit vacated and remanded the 2002 Final Rule to the EPA after determining that the Agency failed to adequately explain the basis for the decision to use vinyl chloride as a surrogate for other HAP. [20] The EPA separately promulgated an area source NESHAP for the PVC and Copolymer Production source category on January 23, 2007, and codified it at 40 CFR part 63, subpart DDDDDD. [21] With the 2012 Final Rule, the EPA promulgated new major source standards for the PVC and Copolymer Production source category at 40 CFR part 63, subpart HHHHHHH and aligned ( printed page 70799) the major and area source NESHAP by revising 40 CFR part 63, subpart DDDDDD. 

 The EPA received multiple petitions for reconsideration of the 2012 Final Rule. [22] To better assess the issues raised for reconsideration, the EPA issued CAA section 114 information collection requests (ICRs) to gather additional information on PVC and copolymer production process vents and wastewater. Additionally, industry stakeholders identified that the EPA used data from outside the PVC and Copolymer Production source category to establish the major and area source total non-vinyl chloride organic HAP process wastewater emission limits. The EPA agreed with industry stakeholders and promulgated the 2015 Final Rule to rescind the total non-vinyl chloride organic HAP process wastewater emission limits for new and existing area sources. [23] In addition, the D.C. Circuit resolved certain contested issues via Mexichem Specialty Resins, Inc. v. EPA [24] and U.S. Sugar Corporation v. EPA, [25] thus mooting the need for the EPA to act on requests to reconsider those aspects of the rule. To further address the remaining reconsideration issues and other technical and editorial corrections, the EPA issued the 2020 Proposal to reconsider certain aspects of the major source PVC NESHAP, including the major source total non-vinyl chloride organic HAP process wastewater emission limits. [26] This final action addresses the proposed reconsideration of the new major source total non-vinyl chloride organic HAP process wastewater emission limit. The EPA intends to address the remaining issues presented in the 2020 Proposal in a separate action. 

The 2012 Final Rule regulates HAP emissions from PVC and copolymer production process units (PVCPU) that produce PVC and copolymers as their primary product(s). A PVCPU is the collection of process components assembled and connected by hard-piping or duct work used to process raw materials to manufacture PVC and/or PVC copolymers and includes, but is not limited to, polymerization reactors, resin stripping operations, resin blend tanks, resin centrifuges, resin dryers, resin product separators, recovery devices, reactant and raw material charge vessels and tanks, holding tanks, mixing and weighing tanks; finished resin product storage tanks or storage silos; finished resin product loading operations; and connected duct and piping. A PVCPU also includes pumps, compressors, agitators, PRDs, sampling connection systems, open-ended valves or lines, valves and connectors, and instrumentation systems.

 PVC is the third most widely produced synthetic polymer in the world and comes in a variety of rigid and flexible forms depending on the application. Vinyl chloride monomer is the primary raw material in PVC and copolymer production, and manufacturers add other components to the polymerization reaction as necessary to modify the properties of the resulting resin to meet product specifications. As such, there are a wide variety of PVC and copolymer resin recipes, and each recipe will result in different HAP present in the PVCPU. There are multiple ways to produce PVC and copolymer resins including bulk polymerization, dispersion polymerization, and suspension polymerization. [27] 

The HAP emission sources at PVC and copolymer production facilities include process vents, storage vessels, equipment leaks, heat exchange systems, wastewater, and stripped resin. While all PVC and copolymer production sources emit vinyl chloride, a PVCPU may also emit other HAP such as benzene, formaldehyde, and toluene depending on the specific resin recipes. The PVC NESHAP includes numeric emission limits for process vents, stripped resin, and wastewater; a mixture of numeric emission limits and work practices for storage vessels depending on the volume and pressure; and work practices for equipment leaks and heat exchange systems.

The EPA identified that this action may affect one potential new major source upon construction and startup. However, this potential new source has not yet commenced construction. While existing sources may reconstruct their PVCPU(s) and become subject to the new source standards, the EPA is unaware of any ongoing reconstruction efforts. As such, the EPA does not anticipate that this action will have any immediate cost or emissions impacts (see section IV of this preamble for additional details).

### B. What changes did we propose for the PVC and Copolymer Production source category in our 2020 Proposal?

 In 2020, the EPA proposed reconsideration of several aspects of the 2012 Final Rule to resolve reconsideration issues that the D.C. Circuit had not addressed. [28] These items included reconsideration of the process vent, stripped resin, and process wastewater emission limits; the process vent emission profile requirements; the pressure vessel provisions; the use of vapor balancing as a method of compliance; and the definition of the affected source. In addition, the EPA proposed technical corrections and clarifications to the alternative emission limit format for compliance with the stripped resin standards, the initial and continuous monitoring requirements for total non-vinyl chloride organic HAP emissions from stripped resin, the fixed and floating roof storage vessel provisions, the equipment leaks practices, and the closed vent system requirements. [29] The EPA also proposed to remove the affirmative defense provisions and to make certain editorial changes to correct errors within the major and area source PVC NESHAP. [30] 

 This action only addresses the proposed reconsideration of the new major source total non-vinyl chloride organic HAP process wastewater emission limit. On this issue, the EPA proposed to remove the major source total non-vinyl chloride organic HAP process wastewater emission limits and the associated testing, monitoring, recordkeeping, and reporting requirements. Relatedly, the EPA also proposed that vinyl chloride can serve as and is a reasonable surrogate for non-vinyl chloride organic HAP in PVC and copolymer production process wastewater because (1) vinyl chloride is the predominant HAP present in all PVC and copolymer production process wastewater streams, and (2) the best performing steam strippers with respect to vinyl chloride are also the most effective at removing non-vinyl chloride organic HAP. The EPA proposed that focusing the emission limit on vinyl chloride via surrogacy rather than on total non-vinyl chloride organic HAP ensured the Agency could identify the best performing wastewater strippers while still controlling non-vinyl chloride organic HAP air emissions. To that end, the EPA proposed that resin recipes determine the presence of other ( printed page 70800) non-vinyl chloride organic HAP in the liquid phase exiting the steam stripper ( i.e., the stripper bottoms). The EPA proposed that the makeup of the stripper bottoms does not necessarily define the overall effectiveness of the steam stripper and stated that wastewater is more likely to retain the non-vinyl chloride organic HAP that steam stripping does not effectively treat. The EPA further proposed that biological treatment will effectively target and reduce those remaining HAP. 

### C. What stakeholder engagement took place following the 2020 Proposal?

 In January 2026, Olin Corporation contacted the EPA to express concern with the new major source total non-vinyl chloride organic HAP process wastewater emission limit in the PVC NESHAP. A summary of this meeting and subsequent calls is in the docket for this action in the memorandum titled Meetings and Calls Between U.S. EPA and the Olin Corporation.

## III. What is included in this final rule, and what is our rationale for our final decisions and amendments for the PVC and Copolymer Production source category?

### A. What final rule amendments are we finalizing based on our reconsideration?

In this action, the EPA is finalizing aspects of the 2020 Proposal concerning the new major source total non-vinyl chloride organic HAP process wastewater emission limit. The EPA is still considering the relevant information and commenter feedback on other portions of the 2020 Proposal and intends to take action on those other portions at a later date.

### B. New Major Source Total Non-Vinyl Chloride Organic HAP Process Wastewater Emission Limit

This section describes what the EPA proposed and what the Agency is finalizing, the EPA's rationale for the final decisions and amendments, and a summary of key comments and responses. The EPA intends to address the remaining comments on the proposed rulemaking when the Agency takes final action on the other aspects of the reconsideration proposal at a later date.

# AGENCY:

Fish and Wildlife Service, Interior.

# ACTION:

Notice of initiation of status reviews.

# SUMMARY:

 We, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, are initiating 5-year status reviews under the Endangered Species Act of 1973, as amended, for 81 species (ESA; 16 U.S.C. 1531 et seq.). A 5-year status review is based on an assessment of the best scientific and commercial data available at the time of the review. We ask the public to submit any new information relevant to the status of any of the species listed in this notice or their habitats. 

# DATES:

These status reviews were announced on November 9, 2026.

# ADDRESSES:

 We will accept new information about these or any listed species at any time. For instructions on how and where to submit information for a species named in these status reviews, see table 1 in the SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION section. Additional information on status reviews is available at https://www.fws.gov/​project/​five-year-status-reviews.

# FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:

 To request information, contact the ( printed page 70893) appropriate person in Table 1 in the SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION section. For general information or to submit information by mail, contact Bradly Potter, via phone at 517-643-7965, via email at R4Recovery@fws.gov, or via U.S. mail at U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, 1875 Century Boulevard, Atlanta, GA 30345. 

Individuals in the United States who are deaf, deafblind, hard of hearing, or have a speech disability may dial 711 (TTY, TDD, or TeleBraille) to access telecommunications relay services. Individuals outside the United States should use the relay services offered within their country to make international calls to the point-of-contact in the United States.

# SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:

We, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, are announcing 5-year status reviews under the ESA for 81 species which include 47 animal species and 34 plant species. A 5-year status review is based on the best scientific and commercial data available at the time of the review. We ask the public to submit at any time any new information relevant to the status of any of the species listed in Table 1 below.

## Why do we conduct 5-year status reviews?

 Under the ESA, we maintain Lists of Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants (which we collectively refer to as the List) in title 50 of the Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) at 50 CFR 17.11 (for wildlife) and 50 CFR 17.12 (for plants). Section 4(c)(2)(A) of the ESA requires us to review each listed species' status at least once every 5 years. Our regulations at 50 CFR 424.21 require that we publish a notice in the Federal Register announcing species under active review. For additional information about 5-year status reviews, refer to our fact sheet at https://www.fws.gov/​project/​five-year-status-reviews.

## What information do we consider in our reviews?

A 5-year status review considers the best scientific and commercial data regarding the species. Such information includes:

(A) Species biology, including but not limited to population trends, distribution, abundance, demographics, habitat requirements, tolerance thresholds, and genetics;

(B) Habitat conditions, including but not limited to amount, distribution, and suitability;

(C) Conservation measures that have been or are planned to be implemented to benefit the species;

(D) Current threats and trends in relation to the five listing factors (as defined in section 4(a)(1) of the ESA (16 U.S.C. 1533(a)(1)); and

(E) Other new information, data, or corrections, including, but not limited to, taxonomic or nomenclature changes, identification of erroneous information contained in the List, and any improved analytical methods.

Any new information will be considered during the 5-year status review and ongoing recovery programs for the species.

## Which species are under review?

When submitting information, please support said information by supplying documentation such as maps; references; methods used to gather and analyze the data; and/or copies of any pertinent scientific journal articles, other publications, reports, or letters by knowledgeable sources. Before including your address, phone number, email address, or other personal identifying information in your submission, you should be aware that your entire submission—including your personal identifying information—may be made publicly available at any time. 

## Authority

 We publish this notice under the authority of the Endangered Species Act of 1973, as amended (16 U.S.C. 1531 et seq.). 

Michael Oetker,

# AGENCY:

Food and Drug Administration, HHS.

# ACTION:

Final amendment; order; notification of partial denial of petition.

# SUMMARY:

The Food and Drug Administration (FDA or we) is partially granting a color additive petition submitted by Environmental Defense Fund et al. (petitioners), by amending our color additive regulations, on the basis of the Delaney Clause, to remove the authorized use of methylene chloride as a diluent in color additive mixtures in inks for marking fruit and vegetables. The petitioners provided data demonstrating that this additive induces cancer in laboratory animals. We are denying the remaining petition requests to remove ethylene dichloride, methylene chloride, and trichloroethylene from the list of authorized extraction solvents for annatto extract, paprika oleoresin, and turmeric oleoresin, because any residue of the solvent would be an impurity in the color additive and such impurities are not subject to the Delaney Clause.

# DATES:

Submit either electronic or written objections and requests for a hearing on the order by December 10, 2026. See section X for further information on the filing of objections.

The https://www.regulations.gov electronic filing system will accept objections until 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time at the end of December 10, 2026. Objections received by mail/hand delivery/courier (for written/paper submissions) will be considered timely if they are received on or before that date.

Because your objection will be made public, you are solely responsible for ensuring that your objection does not include any confidential information that you or a third party may not wish to be posted, such as medical information, your or anyone else's Social Security number, or confidential business information, such as a manufacturing process. # SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:

## Table of Contents:

I. Introduction

II. Background

A. Statutory and Regulatory Background of Color Additive Regulation

B. History of the Color Additive Regulations Where Amendments Are Requested

III. Summary and Context of Determination

IV. Evaluation of Petition

A. 21 CFR 73.1 “Diluents in Color Additive Mixtures for Food Use Exempt From Certification”

B. 21 CFR 73.30 “Annatto Extract”

C. 21 CFR 73.345 “Paprika Oleoresin”

D. 21 CFR 73.615 “Turmeric Oleoresin”

V. Comments Related to the Petition

VI. Conclusion

VII. Public Disclosure

VIII. Analysis of Environmental Impacts

IX. Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995

X. Objections

## I. Introduction

 In the Federal Register of January 11, 2024 (89 FR 1856), we announced that we filed a color additive petition (CAP 4C0327) submitted by Environmental Defense Fund, Breast Cancer Prevention Partners, Center for Environmental Health, Environmental Working Group, and Lisa Lefferts, c/o Lisa Lefferts, Nellysford, VA 22958 (currently c/o Liora Fiksel, 1875 Connecticut Ave. NW, Washington, DC 20009). 

The petition proposed that we amend §§ 73.1 (21 CFR 73.1, “Diluents in color additive mixtures for food use exempt from certification”), 73.30 (21 CFR 73.30, “Annatto extract”), 73.345 (21 CFR 73.345, “Paprika oleoresin”), and 73.615 (21 CFR 73.615, “Turmeric oleoresin”) to remove the use of three specified solvents.

The three solvents that are the subject of this petition are:

1. Ethylene dichloride (Chemical Abstract Service (CAS) No. 107-06-2);

2. Methylene chloride (CAS No. 75-09-2); and

3. Trichloroethylene (CAS No. 79-01-6).

Specifically, the petitioners state these substances have been found to induce cancer in animals and, therefore, are not safe pursuant to section 721(b)(5)(B) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FD&C Act) (21 U.S.C. 379e(b)(5)(B)).

 The notification of petition gave interested parties until March 11, 2024, to submit comments on the filed color additive petition. The petition was made available in the docket. In the Federal Register of May 28, 2026 (91 FR 31680), we reopened the comment period for 30 days to allow for the submission of any updated data and other information over the last two years. 

 This order grants the petition's request to amend the regulations to no longer provide for the use of methylene chloride as a diluent in color additive mixtures in inks for marking fruit and vegetables. This order denies the petition's remaining requests. However, as noted in section VI of this document, FDA is taking action on these remaining requests in response to a separate petition based on industry's abandonment of these uses. ( printed page 72415) 

## II. Background

### A. Statutory and Regulatory Background of Color Additive Regulation

The FD&C Act authorizes us to regulate “color additives” (see section 721(b) of the FD&C Act). The FD&C Act defines “color additive” as a material which is a dye, pigment, or other substance made by a process of synthesis or similar artifice, or extracted, isolated, or otherwise derived, with or without intermediate or final change of identity, from a vegetable, animal, mineral, or other source, and that when added or applied to a food, drug, or cosmetic, or to the human body or any part thereof, is capable (alone or through reaction with another substance) of imparting color (“color” includes black, white, and intermediate grays) thereto (see section 201(t) of the FD&C Act (21 U.S.C. 321(t))). Color additives used in or on a food, drug, cosmetic, or certain medical devices are deemed unsafe and prohibited except to the extent that we approve their use (see section 721(a) of the FD&C Act). Certain color additives must be certified by FDA (see section 721(c) of the FD&C Act).

The FD&C Act provides a process through which any person who wishes to use a color additive in or on food, drugs, certain devices, or cosmetics may submit a petition proposing the issuance of a color additive regulation listing such use with supporting information. A color additive petition may also be submitted to propose the amendment or repeal of any existing color additive regulation (see section 721(b)(5)(C) and (d) of the FD&C Act). In response to a color additive petition, FDA may issue a regulation listing a color additive for use in or on food, drugs, devices, or cosmetics only if it determines that the additive is suitable and safe for such use (see section 721(b)(1) of the FD&C Act).

Under section 721(b) of the FD&C Act, we will not establish a regulation for the use of a color additive if a fair evaluation of the data fails to establish that the proposed use of the color additive, under the conditions of use to be specified in the regulation, will be safe. To determine whether a color additive is safe, the FD&C Act requires FDA to consider, among other relevant factors: (1) probable consumption of, or other relevant exposure from, the additive and of any substance formed in or on food, drugs or devices, or cosmetics because of the use of the additive; (2) cumulative effect, if any, of such additive “in the diet of man or animals,” taking into account the same or any chemically or pharmacologically related substance or substances in such diet; and (3) safety factors recognized by experts “as appropriate for the use of animal experimentation data” (see section 721(b)(5)(A) of the FD&C Act) (referred to as the “general safety clause”). FDA's determination that a color additive is safe means that there is convincing evidence that establishes with reasonable certainty that no harm will result from the intended condition of use of the color additive (§ 70.3(i) (21 CFR 70.3(i))). We refer to this safety standard as “a reasonable certainty of no harm.”

 In addition, section 721(b)(5)(B) of the FD&C Act, often referred to as the Delaney Clause, deems a color additive unsafe under certain circumstances. The Delaney Clause for color additives consists of two parts. The first part (section 721(b)(5)(B)(i) of the FD&C Act) pertains specifically to ingested color additives. The second part (section 721(b)(5)(B)(ii) of the FD&C Act) applies to non-ingested color additives. For purposes of our review of this petition, we reviewed these uses of the solvents ethylene dichloride, methylene chloride, and trichloroethylene under the first part because these uses result in ingestion. Section 721(b)(5)(B)(i) of the FD&C Act states that a color additive shall be deemed unsafe for any use which will or may result in ingestion of all or part of such additive if the additive is found by the Secretary to induce cancer when ingested by man or animal, or if it is found by the Secretary, after tests which are appropriate for the evaluation of the safety of additives for use in food, to induce cancer in man or animal. Courts have concluded that the Delaney Clause is to be interpreted very rigidly. In Public Citizen v. Young, 831 F.2d 1108, 1122 (D.C. Cir. 1987), the court held that Congress intended for the Delaney Clause to be “extraordinarily rigid,” to protect the public from cancer-causing substances without exception, rejecting FDA's argument that a particular color additive should be approved because it did not pose more than a de minimis cancer risk; see also Les v. Reilly, 968 F.2d 985, 986 (9th Cir. 1992) (holding that the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency's (EPA) refusal to revoke regulations permitting the use of certain pesticides, which were regulated as food additives at the time of the court decision and subject to a similarly worded Delaney Clause for food additives, on the grounds that they pose a de minimis cancer risk, is contrary to the provisions of the Delaney Clause). Importantly, however, the Delaney Clause applies to the additive itself and not to constituents (such as nonfunctional chemicals present in the additive) or impurities in the additive. That is, where an additive itself has not been shown to cause cancer but contains a carcinogenic constituent or impurity, the additive is properly evaluated under the general safety clause using risk assessment procedures to determine whether there is a reasonable certainty that no harm will result from the intended use of the additive ( Scott v. FDA, 728 F.2d 322 (6th Cir. 1984)). 

There is a similar Delaney Clause provision for food additives under section 409(c)(3) of the FD&C Act (21 U.S.C. 348(c)(3)), which states that no food additive shall be deemed safe if it is found to induce cancer when ingested by man or animal, or if it is found, after tests which are appropriate for the evaluation of the safety of food additives, to induce cancer in man or animal. In revoking certain authorizations for food additives under the Delaney Clause, FDA stated that the Delaney Clause limits FDA's discretion to determine the safety of food additives. FDA stated that the Delaney Clause prevents FDA from finding a food additive to be safe if it has been found to induce cancer when ingested by humans or animals, “regardless of the probability, or risk, of cancer associated with exposure to the additive or of the extent to which the experimental conditions of the animal study or the carcinogenic mode of action provide insight into the health effects of human consumption and use of the additive in question” (83 FR 50490 at 50492, October 9, 2018).

Section 721(d) of the FD&C Act provides for the issuance, amendment, or repeal of regulations authorizing the use of a color additive, and, among other things, it specifies that the safety provisions of section 721(b)(5) of the FD&C Act apply to such

# ACTION:

Final amendment; order; notification of partial denial of petition.

# SUMMARY:

The Food and Drug Administration (FDA or we) is partially granting a color additive petition submitted by Environmental Defense Fund et al. (petitioners), by amending our color additive regulations, on the basis of the Delaney Clause, to remove the authorized use of methylene chloride as a diluent in color additive mixtures in inks for marking fruit and vegetables. The petitioners provided data demonstrating that this additive induces cancer in laboratory animals. We are denying the remaining petition requests to remove ethylene dichloride, methylene chloride, and trichloroethylene from the list of authorized extraction solvents for annatto extract, paprika oleoresin, and turmeric oleoresin, because any residue of the solvent would be an impurity in the color additive and such impurities are not subject to the Delaney Clause.

# DATES:

 This order is effective January 11, 2027. If any provisions are delayed or stayed by the filing of proper objections, FDA will publish such notification in the Federal Register . Submit either electronic or written objections and requests for a hearing on the order by December 10, 2026. See section X for further information on the filing of objections.

...

Therefore, we are amending the regulation to no longer provide for the use of methylene chloride as a diluent in color additive

...

Our revocation of this authorization is based on a finding under the Delaney Clause that methylene chloride can induce cancer in animals. It is not based on a finding that the intended use is no longer safe under the general safety clause. Upon the effective date of this order (see DATES ), the use of methylene chloride as a diluent in color additive mixtures in inks for marking fruit and vegetables is no longer authorized.

...

The Delaney Clause is applicable to the color additive itself but not to constituents or impurities in the additive. Residues of ethylene dichloride, methylene chloride, and trichloroethylene, when used as an extractant for annatto extract, paprika oleoresin, and turmeric oleoresin, may end up as an impurity in the color additive and would be considered an impurity in the color additive, not a color additive itself. The Delaney Clause applies to color additives, and not to impurities in a color additive. Because the Delaney Clause does not provide a basis for removing these authorizations, FDA is denying the petition's request to remove the authorized uses of ethylene dichloride, methylene chloride, and trichloroethylene in §§ 73.30, 73.345, and 73.615. We note, however, that elsewhere in this issue of the Federal Register , we have published a final order amending the color additive regulations to no longer provide for these uses of ethylene dichloride, methylene chloride, and trichloroethylene because these uses have been abandoned. Therefore, FDA is taking all of the actions requested by the petitioners.

FDA is denying as moot the portion of the petition proposing that the color additive regulations be amended, on the basis of abandonment, to no longer authorize the use of methylene chloride as a diluent in color additive mixtures in inks for marking fruit and vegetables. This request is moot because the authorization for this use has been removed, on the basis of the Delaney Clause, in response to a separate petition.

## Table of Contents
